speechtext:

In light of the fact that farmers in my riding of Brant-and, indeed, across Canada-have come to depend on Canfarm for farm management services that are vital to their farming operations, in light of the fact that farmers across Canada have indicated their willingness to pay fees up to five times higher than at present for these services, and in light of the fact that the federal government has made a considerable investment in Canfarm over the past 12 years, making it one of the best farm management programs in the world, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 28 the Minister of Finance predicted that Canada's trade surplus this year would be $4 billion, and on September 29, when he revealed that our surplus for August was only $186 million, the Canadian dollar declined sharply because the experts felt deceived by the minister's statement. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce predicted a trade surplus of $5 billion this year. Of course, no one pays much attention to his predictions.
My question to the minister is, could he now give the government's considered, best estimate of the likely merchandise trade balance for 1978, keeping in mind that for the first eight months of this year the surplus was $2,084 million which, continued for the rest of the year, would only give us a surplus of $3.1 billion? Can the minister give us the official
Oral Questions
estimate of the merchandise trade surplus, so that the Canadian dollar will not suffer any longer because of ministerial lack of credibility?

Mr. Speaker, I have said that at the time of my budget I will review the forecast which we made some time ago. However, I should like to tell the House of Commons that I am convinced the surplus in trade this year will be at a record level. Last year we had $2.9 billion. It will be substantially more than that this year; it will be a record year.
Hear, hear!

Does the minister still stick to his prediction of June 1, as taken from Hansard, that we had a trade surplus of $3 billion last year and, if the present trend continues, the surplus could be $5 billion this year? Is he still sticking to that? Could he explain how, during the last three months of this year-that is, June, July and August-our trade surplus totalled only $101 million, whereas for the same period last year it totalled $542 million?
In view of these alarming results, how can he justify an estimate of up to $5 billion for the merchandise trade surplus this year, particularly in view of the result of the last three months?

I did not say it would be $5 billion, Mr. Speaker. I said that if the trend remained the same-and, obviously, during the last three months it was not the same- for the over-all year we would have a trade surplus higher than last year and it would be at a record level. I hope the hon. member will recognize that good performance. In fact, Mr. Speaker, in passing let me say that the Canadian dollar, being somewhat weaker, has been of very much help to the fishermen of Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the dollar is now trading at just over 84 cents, which is far below what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said the dollar should be trading at-he said par should be 90 cents-would the minister tell us what is, in fact, the policy of the government? Is it that the dollar should be 90 cents, should par be 90 cents, should it be 84 cents, or 80 cents? What is the minister's policy?

Mr. Speaker, perhaps for the hundredth time since I am the minister, I must say that the policy of the government is to let the Canadian dollar float. The level of the dollar is determined by the market and the Bank of Canada intervenes only to maintain an orderly market.

subtopic: LOSS OF JOBS RESULTING FROM GOVERNMENT CUTBACKS

speechtext:

Prime Minister if he would confirm that an assessment had been made by the government in respect of employment consequences as a result of the more than $2.5 billion in cutbacks announced by the governement. I ask the minister, considering that Informetrica Limited, an economic consulting firm in Ottawa used frequently by the federal government, produced a report today which points out that there will, indeed, be 94,000 jobs lost as a result of the government's cutbacks, is there a federal government assessment showing similar results; and, if so, would he table it?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not aware of such a study by the government. Of course, if the climate improves in Canada there will certainly be more than a mere replacement of jobs by new activities in the private sector.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe I understood correctly what the minister just said. subsubtopic: BUDGETARY REDUCTIONS-RESPONSIBILITY OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, who, a while ago, announced cuts of some $580 million in the unemployment insurance budget, adding that those cuts would have little effect on the provinces.
As we heard yesterday that, as a result of those cuts, British Columbia would have to pay $105 million in welfare; Ontario, $15 million; Newfoundland, $44 million, not to mention Quebec which will probably have to spend $75 million, can the minister tell the House how it is that, when he announced his reductions he did not have those figures at hand or, to say the least, had not advised the provinces that because of reductions they would have to shoulder those heavy financial burdens?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: BUDGETARY REDUCTIONS-RESPONSIBILITY OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the ministers whom I met yesterday concurred with the report that we presented to them. It showed the impact we anticipated the cuts would have on their welfare programs, which were significantly below their worst concerns.
Secondly, in their approach they were throwing everything into the hopper and indicating that this would create an impact on welfare, that people moving from unemployment insurance programs would automatically go to welfare. That, of course, is not in accordance with the facts. But because of their concerns and because of the very fruitful meeting we had yesterday, we are establishing a joint federal-provincial committee to look at the impact as seen from the view of the provinces and the federal government, always remembering that any impact on the welfare program is borne to the extent of 50 per cent by the federal government, in any event, under the Canada Assistance Plan.

speechtext:

We are trying to reduce the gross by $370 million. We informed the provinces that we want to negotiate that kind of cut with them. There was a meeting at the level of deputy ministers.
In my travelling, visiting the various ministers of finance, we will discuss this matter, and we will discuss it further at the meeting in November. We have not said specifically that we would cut this program or that program. We have said that no program will be completely exempted.

subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON FISHERIES' BOUNDARY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the fact that 140 days have elapsed since June 2, the day on which Canada and the United States closed their waters to each other's fishermen, and since there are valuable fisheries and hydrocarbons on Georges Bank, the loss of which would seriously affect the economy of Atlantic Canada, can the minister indicate whether any agreement on an international boundary in this area has been reached? If not, will he briefly inform the House of the present status of negotiations between our two countries?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON FISHERIES' BOUNDARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite difficult, as the hon. member appreciates, to do this briefly in the oral question period. The talks are going amicably but, I fear, not rapidly. In other

words, there is an enormous number of very complex subjects involved, particularly as these relate to the allocation of fish stocks between the two countries. What we decided-and by "we", I mean Secretary of State Vance and myself-in New York two weeks ago was to continue the mandate of our negotiators for a further period, with a view, First of all, to seeing how many of the issues still unresolved can be settled by negotiation, and also to look at the possibilities-I should add, by the way, in consultation with fishing interests and the provinces on both coasts-of referring some of the issues that are still unresolved to arbitration. This would also involve, of course, determining what form that arbitration should take.
I think I can best conclude by re-emphasizing what I have said. There is no ill feeling involved. There is a genuine recognition on both sides of the complexity of the issue and an anxiety to ensure that all parties, including fishing interests in both countries, the provinces and the states, are all fully involved and fully advised of the direction the talks are taking. As soon as there is something more specific, I will be more than pleased to let the House know.

subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON FISHERIES' BOUNDARY
speechtext: In view of the fact that one of the negotiators, Mr. Cadieux, has been assigned other responsibilities, can the minister indicate whether this will have any effect on our future negotiations?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON FISHERIES' BOUNDARY
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, it will not-not in the immediate future, in any event. If the talks were to proceed beyond a matter of a few months, then it might very well do so. However, the arrangements for his new assignment took into account the possibility that he would continue to be involved in these negotiations. I would hope that by the end of the year, let us say, if not before, we will at least have the framework for further progress in identifying those issues which can be negotiated and, most important perhaps, trying to put into place an interim arrangement in the event that we have to go to international arbitration or something of that sort on the larger questions of great complexity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. It concerns the current armed forces recruiting program and the costly series of television advertisements which the minister's department has been airing.
In view of the fact that during fiscal year 1976-1977 the armed forces accepted only one of every ten applicants, and only one out of every 25 contacts, and considering that during this time of high unemployment many interested men and women have been applying to the armed forces through the normal recruiting program, can the minister tell the House how much this current advertising campaign is costing for every recruit actually enrolled in the armed forces? Can he
October 12, 1978

also tell us why, at a time of announced cutbacks, this costly program should be undertaken at all, considering that so many highly-motivated job-seekers commit themselves to the recruitment process only to be turned down later after a long and expensive process?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: ARMED FORCES RECRUITING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the advertising program was, of course, contracted for long before the current cutbacks. Nevertheless, it does give us an opportunity to be highly selective. We have always had a high proportion of people applying for service in our armed forces because of the excellent reputation they have, the excellent training young men and women receive and the excellent career opportunities they have. This means we are able to be more selective.
We are increasing the number of people in the forces over-all. It is true that attrition, at the same time, has been reduced. We will, however, have in future years a need for more people. We want to maintain that interest among them and maintain the high standards which we presently have so that we can be selective and get the very best people.

Mr. Speaker, on both counts the answer is yes; but, once again, it is difficult to give all the details. I met with the delegation which was in Ottawa on Tuesday. I indicated that I
Oral Questions
will raise this issue with the foreign ministers of the Western Five on the Security Council this weekend in Pretoria, so that in terms of the follow-on action to which the hon. member refers, I think he can rest assured that it is in hand.

Our constitutional challenge is twofold: first, we must put an end to the deadlock in which Ottawa is opposed to all the provinces on the matter of the sharing of powers. This Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has had ten years to design the constitution he wants. He has changed the constitution and he did so in reserving more and more powers for Ottawa.

I am sure that we will follow through on this agreement in less than six months after we are elected. Rather than once again trying to jump from one subject to the other in order to go into all the areas which the Leader of the Opposition has led us through, I will try to divide the remarks I have to make into two areas, the economy first, and then the subject of national unity.
The Leader of the Opposition submitted that on unemployment and on inflation in particular this government has a great deal of explaining to do, and I propose to give those explanations in the course of the next few minutes. On unemployment the Tories say that they would put Canada back to work. Well, the simple fact is that Canada has not stopped working. Canada has created more employment in the past ten years than any other industrial society.
In each of the past ten years we created an average of more than a quarter of a million jobs, and that rate is unequalled anywhere in the industrialized world. Let me give some figures. I have several to give. I would say that they concern the 15 most industrialized countries. They concern those countries with which we do about 90 per cent of our trade. Therefore, they are the most important countries. They do not include Kuwait and Bahrain, but they do include the countries with which we do 90 per cent of our trade, by and large.
These figures are OECD figures and, when possible, I have taken the period from 1968 to 1977. In some cases the OECD figures are not provided for 1968 and 1969. In those cases I start in 1970, but we do know the Canadian figures, and we do know that the tables would be even better if we had the figures for all the other countries because Canada did well indeed in those first two years, 1968 and 1969.
Percentage change in employment from 1970 to 1977, Canada, rate of growth in employment: 23 per cent. The next closest is the United States with 15 per cent, then Australia, and then those countries about which we say a great deal of good and which are sometimes named as models for Canada. Sweden is at 5 per cent as compared to our 23 per cent; Japan, 5 per cent; West Germany, minus 6 per cent; and Switzerland, minus 11 per cent. Probably they rank very high in terms of the standard of living. The reason is very simple; not only did the number of jobs not grow in those countries but it was actually reduced by 5 per cent or 11 per cent. Why was that? For the very simple reason that workers in those countries, who came from Turkey, Portugal, Spain or Yugoslavia, were sent back home when the economy slowed down, so naturally there were fewer unemployed in those countries, the governments did not need as stimulative an economic policy and therefore were better able to protect their currency.
The Leader of the Opposition understands, I am sure, that if that were the situation in Canada, if we could actually reduce our work force, it would be relatively easy to show a better exchange rate. But when we must find jobs for the fastest growing labour force in the world, it is a different problem from that in the countries I have mentioned. Therefore, Canada, in terms of the employment growth rate, is the best in the world. That is true for those seven years and it is equally

true if we take the difficult years of the post OPEC crisis from 1974 to 1977. We still lead the world in terms of job creation.
Let us consider the rate of growth of the real domestic product. In that respect Canada is third. The annual average between 1968 and 1977 has increased by 4.5 per cent a year. Ahead of us are Japan and France; we come third before Germany, Australia, Finland, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. If we take the three difficult years, from 1974 to 1977, we see that Canada comes second just after Norway.
Let us consider the growth in industrial production which shows that Canada has been at work these past years. In industrial production the OECD base year is 1970. In the percentage increase we come second, right after Norway. Norway is at 38 per cent; we have a 32 per cent increase in industrial production since 1970. What has happened? We have grown very fast, we have a faster job creation than any other country, but still we have an unacceptably high unemployment. Thank heavens it has not increased since the month of June, but it is still much too high, that is certain. Why is it too high and what can be done about it? Once again this is where you should not use your imagination but rather your reasoning.
If you look at the rate of growth of the labour force, you will find that between 1968 and 1977 of all the countries in the world Canada's labour force has grown the fastest. We are followed by the United States, Norway, Australia. Sweden's rate of growth in the labour force is down at 10 per cent as compared to our 33 per cent; Japan is at 7 per cent; once again Germany has a negative growth rate and so has Switzerland. Therefore, even though we created jobs at a faster rate than any other society, our labour force has increased faster than in any other industrial society, so naturally the result is a high rate of unemployment.
It is said sometimes that the government could have foreseen that. Obviously this situation is due to three things: it is due to the birth rate. After the Korean was there was a baby boom. We knew that all these young people would be coming onto the labour force in the 1970s. Second, it is due to the immigration rate, and we are happy to continue to receive immigrants in this country.

We have not heard the Tory policies on the subjects I will discuss, but first let us look at the facts. We know that for the past two months the rate of inflation has been slowly coming down. Also we know that from August to September inflation was wrestled to the ground for one month. 1 dare say it will not be a permanent victory, but we will continue fighting in the manner which I will indicate.
In order to set the record straight when we talk about standard of living and cost of living, let us look at some of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development figures. The standard of living is expressed in terms of real disposable purchasing power. In 1968 we were second, right after the United States. They had $4,679 and we had $3,516. Eight years later, the latest date for which we have figures, we are still second. I am talking of constant dollars, obviously Canadian dollars brought to the 1971 base. In 1976 the United States were at $4,258 and Canada was at $4,082. Thus, we were still second, and away ahead of Switzerland, the Netherlands, Germany, Norway, Japan, Italy, but perhaps not ahead of Kuwait. I am not sure, I do not have the figures for Kuwait. If we are talking of real disposable purchasing power, probably we are pretty well ahead of Kuwait. For something which costs perhaps $50 in this country, one will pay perhaps $300 in that country. If one is not the Emir himself, who will have a little bit of difficulty maintaining his purchasing power.
The United States is listed first on the cost of living index. Putting that country on the basis of one hundred and comparing the cost of living of various countries to the United States in any of the years 1968, 1970, 1974, 1976 or 1978, Canada is always in the top little group. Let us take the two years to which reference is always made. In 1968 we were second. The cost of living index in the United States was one hundred and the cost of living index comparatively in Canada was one hundred and one. In 1978, ten years later, the United States

was 100 and Canada was 102. We are still second, and away ahead of France, Germany, Switzerland, and Japan. Japan was 165 compared to our 102. Though the figures on inflation are not nice and we would rather have a lower rate of inflation, obviously the result of these years of inflation indicates that Canada has done immensely better than most of the other industrialized countries.

We pay $19 for that basket in Canada. There is one country ahead of us by one cent. That country is Australia where the basket costs $18.99. After us, in terms of food prices, come the United States, United Kingdom, and further on Germany, Sweden, Denmark, Japan, and all these other countries. Thus, in terms of food also we are among the winners.
I should like to refer to another index, real personal disposable income.

Therefore, taking 1968 as 100, the real personal disposable income per capita in Canada has risen from 100 to 151.90. In other words, we have increased our real personal disposable income per capita. That is gross earnings plus all which is received in terms of transfer payments, minus all taxes. We have gained some 50 per cent. Compared to the United States, in that country it went from 100 to 124. Once again we are ahead of everyone and we are doing very well in terms of real wealth.

Other industries are referred to in the census and by Statistics Canada. I will refer to a few in order to show that over the past ten years this country has not really seen itself reduced from riches to rags. Let us look at a few of these indices, first in relation to personal expenditures on consumer goods and services.
In the case of food, beverages and tobacco, our expenditure on these items compared to our total expenditures has gone down from 21 per cent to 19 per cent. In the case of rent our expenditure has gone down from 19 per cent to 17 per cent.
October 12, 1978

The percentage has gone up in respect of recreation, entertainment, education and cultural services.
There is another way of expressing this, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is constantly reminding us of this. It relates to the percentage of disposable income spent on food, the assumption being that when you are wealthy you spend a smaller proportion of your income on food than when you are poor. This index puts the United States first and Canada second, away ahead of most of these so-called model countries. In the United States 12 per cent of disposable income is spent on food whereas in Canada it is 13 per cent. This means, according to this index, that we in Canada have a surprisingly advantageous situation.
Let me refer to the index in relation to households. In 1968 some 91 per cent of households in Canada had hot and cold running water. Seven years later this had increased to 97 per cent. In relation to the number with baths or showers, in 1968 there were 90 per cent and in 1977 there were 97 per cent. In 1968 some 29 per cent of households had home freezers. This increased to 47 per cent in 1977.
The opposition can look at these indices. I will send them over if hon. members are interested. These cover the point about flush toilets, sewers, and everything else.

Hon. members will see that we are not really caught in the vortex that they seem to be describing. Indeed, in Canada the facts are that in spite of inflation we are doing well, indeed.
Why do we have a high cost of living? Obviously there are many reasons. We cannot say at this time that this is inflation generated in Canada. We have found that from the first half of 1975, when wage settlements on a yearly basis were at a rate of 22 per cent, they have dropped to something in the order of 7 per cent, with a cost of living of 8 per cent to 9 per cent. That means that at this time inflation is coming in from outside, very simply because of the high cost of things we import, and very simply because of the lowered value of the dollar, which means Canada is paying more for everything it imports.
In the face of this situation the Leader of the Opposition says the throne speech contains nothing and the government has done nothing. Throughout the month of August we announced cuts in government spending. From projected spending in this fiscal year we are taking $500 million. From expenditures projected for the next fiscal year we are taking away $2 billion.
In relation to growth in the public sector, and I am not talking of the provinces or the municipalities, in the present year and the next we are growing at a rate that is less than as fast as the economy itself is growing. The civil service in the past two years and in this year has been growing at less than 1 per cent, and next year that growth will be zero.
We have taken a very difficult decision in respect of Bill C-28 which was brought in during the last parliament and
The Address-Mr. Trudeau
which will be brought in again during this parliament in a modified form. What is the position of the opposition in respect of this bill, which really is a follow-up to the commitment made by the ten premiers and myself in February when we decided that total compensation in the public sector should not lead that of the private sector? We are putting that in the form of a bill and will ask the Leader of the Opposition and his party to support it. I understand the NDP will not support us, but it will be interesting to see whether the Leader of the Opposition has a position in this regard. He will complain about inflation, but we want to know whether he will support the government's policy which has been announced but which he feigns not to know.
What is his position on this policy in view of all these matters of restraint? I can predict now what it is. Every time we bring in a bill, and there will be many, cutting federal expenditures, members of the opposition complain. Already today we have heard the complaint that we are cutting too much in the wrong places. The opposition always find some reason not to support the expenditure restraint by the federal government, but never will they propose an equivalent amount to be cut in other areas. We will just watch for their support in this particular respect.
In the face of inflation in the past this government has taken what I would say is a very compassionate stand: indexing of various pensions including family allowances, old age pensions, veterans' pensions and so on. This has been a major step in protecting those people in the weaker element of our society against the evils of inflation. These measures have cost a great deal of money.
We continued these measures of restraint in the month of August by cutting expenditures in some areas, taking away from those who have and who do not need quite as much. In this way we have been able to increase the guaranteed income supplement by $20 per month per household, and this will affect some 3,300,000 pensioners. In respect of family allowances, and I will explain it once again because the people out there watching television do not seem to have understood it properly-

The principle of redistribution is to take from them who have in order to give to those who do not. In the case of the Leader of the Opposition he has two kinds of redistribution in mind. We have already heard talk about one, and that is redistribution of federal powers to the provinces. That can be quite painless for the Leader of the Opposition. We have had an example of the other kind of redistribution, namely, the housing policy of which he is so proud. Under this housing policy, them that has gets, and I think we can give a few examples of that.
Again let me put some housing facts on record because the opposition would seem to indicate that in this area of housing we have not done enough. Let me just indicate once again that of the 15 most industrialized countries of the world Canada was second in housing starts from 1970 to 1977. The index shows Belgium first with 152, Canada second with 126, and the United States, with its mortgage deductibility, at 116, fewer housing starts than in Canada. Norway, Japan, and the other countries follow. We have such a good record because of good Liberal housing policy in Canada.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

I understand the Leader of the Opposition wants to save $20 million by abolishing the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, but he should consider what has been achieved in the past ten years since we set up this ministry. The central objective of federal housing policy has been to increase the supply of all types of shelter and to maximize individual choice and to stabilize prices.
Aided by a variety of tax incentives and a near tripling of CMHC budgets from $655 million in 1968 to $1,890 million in 1977, Canada's housing industry has produced over 2.1 million starts since 1968, the best record in our history and the best record, after Belgium, of any industrialized society. In the latest four-year period, 1973 to 1977, Canada annually produced approximately 250,000 starts, far better than any other four-year period in our history. For instance, if you take from 1963 to 1967 there were 155,000 housing starts, and in 1958 to 1962 there were 134,000 starts compared, once again, to 248,000 starts for the period 1973 to 1977. That is well ahead of the Economic Council's goal of one million over five years.
Federal government programs were essential in achieving this number of starts. The proportion of starts with some National Housing Act subsidy increased from 6 per cent in 1968 to over 40 per cent in 1977. It is because of that large increase in starts since 1973 that prices for houses have stabilized. In 1976-77 the price of existing homes only increased by 3.9 per cent. There has been a housing policy in this country, Mr. Speaker. It has created houses in a number exceeding any other period in our history, and, I repeat, better than any other industrialized society with the exception of Belgium.
I understand that the Leader of the Opposition and his party are flailing around asking themselves what they can do in

order to redistribute wealth in their way. They do not like the way the Minister of Finance is doing it. They do not like the way this government is doing it. So, what are they going to do to redistribute wealth? Let us take a look at the practical application of their policies. For instance, there are the renters in Canada. They are not a small group for there are 2.4 million householders in this country who rent their shelter, 37 per cent of all households. These renters are not the rich people. Approximately 60 per cent of all renters make $10,000 or less, and many of these are older Canadians or families which are starting out.
Let us take, for example, one senior citizen, a widow who is retired and renting, and what does she get from this Tory tax policy? She gets zero, Mr. Speaker-not one cent.

Let us now look at the man in the low middle income bracket who owns a home and who has no mortgage. This is not a small group either. There are 4 million householders in Canada who own their homes, and one half of these have no mortgage. That means that 2 million out of 4 million home owners have no mortgage. They are not going to benefit from this promise. What does the Tory promise say to this person, this low middle income earner who has a house but no mortgage? It says, "If you want this tax break, well, go out and mortgage your home." Of course, if they do that this will put the expenditure way above the $1.6 billion which is the calculated Tory figure.

I did want to talk about the problem of national unity at some length but I think I will save part of my remarks for some other occasion, because I have taken a lot of the time of the House. I would briefly contrast our approach here again to that of the opposition, because the Leader of the Opposition did say some words about his approach to the problem of national unity and I have already commented on that a little bit.
Let me first say that we do give very high priority to the problem of national unity and to the remedies we propose, for a very simple reason. It is that the Canadian economy will not attain its full potential unless this problem of disjointed unity, of political uncertainty, is solved, and unless an investor, whether he is going to invest in Windsor or Winnipeg, knows he is investing in a country of 23 million people, not of 23 million minus six million. This is very important for the economy.
To those people who say, "Why are you tinkering with the situation? Why are you spending your time talking about national unity when there are jobs to be found and inflation on your back", that is the answer. Economic uncertainty flows from political uncertainty. It is extremely important that on all sides of the House we tackle this problem with great urgency. [Translation]
The second reason why this problem must be solved immediately was stated just two days ago by the Premier of the pro ince of Quebec, Mr. Levesque, who was speaking in the National Assembly, and I quote:
One thing for sure anyway, we do not see anything but sovereignty-association as a solution likely to break the vicious circle in which are trapped two different people.
Well, that is what we have always maintained, Mr. Speaker. Quebeckers, like westerners and maritimers, want a solution to this constitutional imbroglio which has been dragging in this country ever since 1927. Quebeckers are anxious to see this parliament not only grapple with this problem of the constitution, but solve it once and for all because we know, Mr. 
Speaker, and all surveys bear this out, that the option of a renewed federalism is to be preferred to any other option for Quebeckers, including of course separation or sovereignty-association.
Quebeckers want a renewed federalism, a new constitution. They are anxious to get results, and they prefer that solution to sovereignty-association. And because the people in Quebec will be called upon to express their opinion in a referendum to be held by the provincial government presumably within a year, we must in the meantime be able to show the province of Quebec that after 51 years of efforts we have finally made some progress, and that is why it is urgent to implement the government's program.
The Leader of the Opposition talked of confrontation, he said that the federal government wants to move too fast, that he, the Leader of the Opposition, would sit down with the provinces, discuss their agenda, start with the division of powers, because that is what concerns them. Has he any guarantee that eight, nine or ten provinces will agree with him on a division of powers within a year or two? The only guarantee he can have, of course, is that if he agrees to give the provinces all the powers and all the jurisdictions they want, if he wants to dismantle the federal government, Mr. Speaker, if he wants to turn the federal government into a vacuum, give the provinces all the powers, of course, he will agree in no time with the provinces on the division of powers. But we know that issue was discussed for three years, from 1968 to 1971, and as the proposals were not forthcoming-and I am talking basically about provincial proposals because the government made several proposals to improve the division, including those I mentioned earlier-the provinces, for the sake of peace and quiet, said: Well, let us get it over with and try, in Victoria at least, to repatriate the constitution and find an amending formula. Now, the Leader of the Opposition says: Hey, hold your horses! Let us take our time! Let us not act too hastily. We have to discuss with the provinces, so no confrontation. I am not for confrontation. I want a solution to be found, but once again, I remind the Leader of the Opposition and all those who are listening that the people in Quebec will have to vote within a year on the various options, and unless we have a renewed federalism to propose, I can guarantee the Leader of the Opposition that federalism is in for a rough time.
The Leader of the Opposition wants to begin with the division of powers because the provinces said that they want to begin with the division of powers. Does he have even the slightest hope that he will get the ten provinces to agree on a new division of powers within the next little while? He shakes his head yes, Mr. Speaker. He is saying that Mr. Levesque will agree on renewing our federalism rather than pursue his option of souverainete independance.

He is going to set aside the proposition to give greater representation to the west and to the east in the institutions of the central government. He is going to set aside linguistic guarantees in order to pursue something, when he should know at the outset that the premier of Quebec will not consent. If he is looking for unanimity, as the premiers suggested at Regina last August that they were looking for, he will not find it. He will not find it this year, and he will not find it next year. All I am saying is that it is important that the Supreme Court of this country has the confidence of Canadians from every region. It is time that we got on with the job of finding ways by which that confidence can be established. We should not sweep that under the carpet too, and say that we will discuss division of powers, which will take us years and years and years. It is important before then to establish the
The Address-Mr. Trudeau
Supreme Court which corresponds to the values for which all Canadians stand.
It is not vital to me whether Her Majesty is formally described in the new constitution as The Sovereign Head of State, or as Her Majesty the Queen, or as the Sovereign of Canada, or in any other way. We have indicated many times that our intention was not to change the role of the monarchy. We indicated that as far back as 1968 when we published the white paper on the constitution. We have repeated it constantly since then that that was our intention.
At one point when we were writing a new constitution we had to say something about the Queen. I think the opposition would have been the first to complain if we had written a new constitution without mentioning the Queen. Therefore we had to put in something. We had our drafters put the description of the situation of today as they see it under constitutional law in the best language they could. This is what they attempted to write, and this is what we want to be in the constitution.
I know some people on the other side who would like to write in what the position was of the Queen in Queen Anne's day, but this is not the position of this government. We want to describe the situation today following the 1947 letters patent which gave to the Governor General the power to exercise Her Majesty's prerogatives which were transferred in final resort to the Governor General about a year and half ago. This we want to put in the constitution. We are repeating, Mr. Speaker, and we have said it since 1968, that this is the intention. The intention was explained to Her Majesty at Buckingham Palace by the then minister of justice, and she saw it that way too. The people who are hollering "the monarchy" in this country are the people on that side of the House who are using it as a political football.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: With a deadline.

That is exactly what we said in the last session that we will bring it in for first reading only, we will set up a parliamentary committee to study it, we will ask the premiers to study it in the provinces, and we will ask them to come back with better wording, if they have it. If they want to revise it, improve it, fine. If they want a new division of powers, fine. Let us hear what they want to propose.
I see the Leader of the Opposition suggesting that we are the ones now. He will wait for us to propose some new division of powers. We are not asking for a new division of powers. I understand it is his party. It is the provinces that are asking for a division of powers. They have made some proposals. We will study them. I have already written to the premiers in that sense. We will make some counter-proposals. We will show that in some instances it is important for the federal government to have powers that are now exercised by the provinces because we believe that Canada must maintain a strong government if it is going to remain united.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
All I am saying is, let's get on with it, let's act. For 51 years, under six different prime ministers, the national government and the provincial governments have tried to tackle the problem of the constitution. They have always come up with failure. If people are fed up with politicians discussing the constitution, it is not because they do not think it is important. It is because they think the politicians should get on with it, finish the job, and not discuss it for another 50 years. That is the position of this government. That

is why we have set deadlines which we will do our best to meet. That is why we will stick with them.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am not sure of the position of the Leader of the Opposition. I do know they brought out a blue paper called "Constitution and National Unity" in April, 1978. On page one of this paper they said "the legitimacy of the existing constitution has been substantially eroded."
They go on to propose what? They go on to propose essentially constitutional changes, not division of powers. Let the Leader of the Opposition read his own position paper. They proposed institutional changes like we did in Bill C-60. They suggested we were copying them at that time because this seemed to be a good wicket to be on.
They talked about the House of the Provinces. It is our House of the Federation. They talked about federal-provincial conferences and the need to institutionalize them. They talked about appointments-another victory at Kingston. At Kingston the Leader of the Opposition gained from the premiers the right for them to name people to the Supreme Court and to federal bodies like the CBC and so on. That was another great victory.
This is what they talked about in their paper on national unity in April, 1978. They talked about the Supreme Court. They said later "we will talk about language rights, later we will publish things on human liberties, later we will talk about the division of powers, our phase II."
What happened? The premiers got together in Regina in 1978. They said they did not want to talk about the Senate, the Supreme Court, and federal-provincial relations. They said they wanted to talk about the division of powers. What did the opposition party do? They simply put out another paper in September, 1978, called "The Process of Constitutional Change" in which they denounce this frantic haste which is unwise. They said it was unacceptable for the federal government to proceed with the very matters that in April they were saying we should proceed with.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: As soon as the provinces say they want to discuss the division of powers, "Right on, Premier Lougheed," says the Leader of the Opposition, "Right on, Premier Davis, ready, aye, ready, we will discuss whatever you want, we will forget the other."

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In the September paper called "The Process of Constitutional Change", they not only reverse their position from April, but they reverse it between page 5 and page 13. On page 5 they talk about "the fundamental silliness of the Trudeau government's position which is pretending to act unilaterally under section 91(1)".
Because the premiers have said, "You cannot exercise your powers which are recognized under the BNA Act under sec-

tion 91(1)," the Leader of the Opposition says we cannot exercise those powers, it is silly of the Trudeau government to try to do it.
The Leader of the Opposition is complaining about federal interference in provincial jurisdictions. Was there any greater interference ever heard of in Canada than the provinces telling us that we cannot exercise a jurisdiction under section 91(1) given to the federal government? If that is not interference, what is?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The provinces have said, "Unless there is some kind of unanimity, some consensus"-they use both words-"you should not use your right to amend the federal constitution." Nobody has ever contested the right of the provincial governments under section 92(1) to change their constitutions. If they want, they can sit down and write there shall be a Queen, there shall be a form of cabinet government, there shall be a legislative assembly, there shall be courts, there shall be an administration and so on. They can do it. But according to this party over here, we cannot do it. We cannot write a constitution which says there will be a Queen, there will be a Governor General, there will be a cabinet government responsible to parliament, there will be two Houses and one will be constituted in this way and the other in that way, and there will be courts. They say we cannot write a constitution for us which is authorized under section 91(1), but they can do it for themselves.
This is indeed a queer view of the centralized powers under section 91(1). I have heard there is a kind of chicken that lays a lot of wonderful eggs. Maybe the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) can tell me more about it. There is only one problem. After it has laid the eggs, it turns around and eats them.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: After laying a very, very big egg, covering very many pages with a very learned argument about why we should not use section 91(1) and why we should not act unilaterally, the Leader of the Opposition, on the last page, comes forth as he did in his speech, and says he is going to show leadership if there is any confrontation, you can rely on him to stand up to them. There is a little weaseled phrase on the last page of this learned page which says "Clearly there are areas where the federal government can act alone, and if necessary we will do so."

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, they sure did stand up to the provinces. We saw how they stood up to them in Kingston. Let us see how they stood up to them on some other occasions. Take the offshore mineral rights. We know this has been contested in this country for at least 12 years. There was a Supreme Court decision. Finally, after months and even years of negotiation between this government and the three maritime provinces and Newfoundland, which wanted to have 100 per cent of the
The Address-Mr. Trudeau
resources on the offshore, and the courts seem to have decided otherwise, at least on the west coast, we stood up for the federal government, as it is our duty to do, to stand up for federal rights under the constitution.
There are premiers who stand up for provincial rights. That is their duty. That is their job. That is what they are elected for. I think the Leader of the Opposition has chosen the wrong House in which to sit. He should be sitting in the provincial Houses standing up for the provincial governments.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
After years of negotiation we put together an agreement with the three maritime premiers suggesting a division of the resources. It was not a judgment of jurisdiction, just a fair division of resources, actually a very generous one for the provinces. After it was put together, it was signed by the three maritime premiers and myself.
A new Conservative premier has now been elected in Nova Scotia. There is a federal by-election now, and the Leader of the Opposition went there and said, "If you want 100 per cent, we will tear up this agreement," which was signed formally in these very parliament buildings a couple of years ago, "and we will give you 100 per cent." That was one example of him standing up to the provinces. If he has to, he will stand up to them and give them 100 per cent.
Let us consider another example, lotteries. I know the history of this very well because it was back in 1967 that I introduced amendments to the Criminal Code to make lotteries legal in Canada. Incidentally, the province of Alberta was the province from which I received the greatest number of letters. Albertans were scandalized because I was introducing an "immoral" system. In Quebec there were other issues. In Manitoba the issue was gun legislation, but in Alberta the issue was lotteries. Some ten years later we tried to make a deal with the provinces. We wanted to share the lotteries, but the provinces wanted 100 per cent. Who does the Leader of the Opposition support? The provinces, of course. Why should the federal government have its lottery when the provinces want to have 100 per cent? Why should we have anything, even if it is only to help sports and amateur sports? Why should we have anything of this?
The Leader of the Opposition takes a very firm position. Using his own words, he will stand up for federal rights, but he says that the lotteries should be 100 per cent the provinces. Fortunately, the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) was able to come to an arrangement with the provinces. There will be a shared arrangement. I do not know if it is going to stick. You never know, because the new premier of Nova Scotia might meet with the Leader of the Opposition, and he might unstick it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: In very simple terms, the Leader of the Opposition accused us of infringing provincial rights, invading provincial jurisdiction and so forth. What happened? We said to the provinces that we would cut income taxes in our jurisdiction, federal income taxes, if the provinces would do something in their jurisdictions. Nobody was invading anybody's jurisdiction. We were saying, "We will do this, if you do that". Eight of the provinces said "Fine". Mr. Parizeau said: "I cannot give you an answer. I will tell you later, after your budget". So after the budget he said: "I do not want to do what you ask, but I want you to give the money as if I had done it". Who was invading whose jurisdiction? We were cutting our taxes, provided the provinces would do something. One province said it would not do anything, but it still wanted us to cut taxes in that province. We were still being told what to do with our federal income tax, but not in exchange for a deal or as a quid pro quo. Unilaterally we were being told how we should arrange our budget. A fight ensued, and we kept hearing from the Leader of the Opposition that not only was Mr. Levesque supporting Mr. Parizeau, but even Mr. Ryan was supporting Mr. Parizeau. So naturally the Leader of the Opposition supported Mr. Parizeau too. He takes not only the position of the provincial premier but also that of the leader of the opposition in that province.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Alberta wants international prices for its oil. Ontario wants lower prices. So does New Brunswick, and I suppose now so will Nova Scotia. They do not want to pay the international price for Alberta oil. They do not want this high price to be applied all across Canada. There is division. We have managed to settle these matters in the past several years. There have been many negotiations. When the Leader of the Opposition was on the back benches he naturally supported the premier of his province, but now that he is the leader of a party, he cannot support one premier against the other, so he does not support either. He just says: "You figure it out amongst yourselves; I will not take a position. Let the federal government do something and I will be with you, Brother Lougheed, and with you, Brother Davis".

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

That would please Brother Davis, but it would not please Brother Lougheed. Can we ask the Leader of the Opposition to stand firm on this in the interests of the people of Canada? Who will he support? I remember a sixteenth century divine about whom it was said that when he spoke he exhausted time and encroached upon eternity. I will not do that. I think I will just wind up by saying that this is a time when the whole industrialized world is coming to grips with very difficult economic problems. Our own country is trying to solve these problems and, as I demonstrated, it is performing better than most, better than all, actually, if we consider the over-all total of performances.
At this difficult time we have a Leader of the Opposition and an official opposition unable or unwilling to make any of the hard choices. We have an official opposition which tries to evade its responsibility and blame the government for everything. The Leader of the Opposition talks about the Speech from the Throne and his anxiety about getting into government. The official opposition will have to learn how to accept some responsibilities. It will have to learn to do so in economic matters and in matters of national unity.
It will have to learn to accept its responsibilities in some of the areas which were referred to in the opening remarks of the Leader of the Opposition, such as matters of national security. When a member of his party was asked by the deputy commissioner of the RCMP to hand over secret documents belonging to the RCMP, the publication of which would be a danger to the security system of this country and to the operation of the RCMP, the Leader of the Opposition turned a blind eye and said, "I do not want to get involved in this". He does not have the courage to accept his responsibility in important matters like that, but he will stand up and talk about his anxiety about coming into government. Let me just say that this government accepts its responsibilities. Sometimes that does mean confrontation. Sometimes it does mean having to say no to the provinces, to labour, to big business or even to the opposition, but we accept our responsibilities.
If the people of this country listen to the siren song of the Leader of the Opposition, who seems to say, "Change the government, you have nothing to lose," let me answer that the people of Canada have everything to lose if they put into power a party which has no confidence in this country, no confidence in its ability to overcome its difficulties and which does not believe that the federal government has the right to lead all the people of this nation, even through the difficult problems which are put to them.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in my view we have heard the best possible demonstration we could have had in ten years of why the country is in so much difficulty.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I say completely sincerely that if ever we had a display of misguided intelligence, that was it. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has made an interesting distinction which I will turn around on him in just a minute. Today, at the opening of his highly disparaging speech about the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), he launched into a personal assault making reference to the fact that the Leader of the Opposition was using notes. Of course, he himself spent a good part of his time using notes. It is all right when on one side of the House an arrogant, condescending and aggressive Prime Minister does one thing, but when someone on this side does it, somehow it is unacceptable.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, come on.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Come on yourself. Look at your side for a minute.
Then the Prime Minister went on to say that he had studied some psychology and had learned that a distinction existed between reason and imagination. He put his hands in his pockets and said, yes, that was a good distinction, and the Leader of the Opposition was very good on imagination but
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
was not so good on intelligence. That was really the gist of his argument.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That's the truth.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is personal vindictiveness and a great way to "unite" this country! But that is what we got from the Prime Minister. He has taken the intelligence with which he was gifted and has governed this country for ten years, but had he used that intelligence, that is there and that is real, to mould support? Has he brought people together to try to build an exciting and decent nation? No. The only time the Prime Minister uses that intelligence is when he is in battle. We saw it in 1972, we saw it in 1974, and for the first time in four years we saw it here today. Suddenly he came alive. Why? Because he likes to fight. The Prime Minister likes to combine two contradictory attitudes: that of a philosopher and that of John Wayne. I say to him that this is a totally undesirable combination for a prime minister of a country.
Let me show what it was all about. He said that the Leader of the Opposition was not good with his facts. I will bring out a few for the Prime Minister to show how, through his distorted, twisted, misleading and false set of facts, quite a different picture will emerge from the one he tried to convey. Two can play that game. The Prime Minister has had responsibility for this nation for ten years, and that is the relevant question, as he knows. But of course he likes to win arguments. He does not like to convince, persuade, lead or give support because he is doing the good or decent thing, but he does like to be clever and win arguments.
That is just the opposite of serious statesmanship or serious philosophy. He trotted out that old canard about job creation and said that Canada leads in job creation. He compared us with other countries. But what he did not tell us was that, unlike many countries with which he was making the comparison, we have had thousands of immigrants every year. So it would seem that we would have to create a few more jobs than would other countries. Also, the other countries had lower birth rates-he did make an allusion to that-and therefore they did not have to create the same number of jobs.
The relevant economic indicator is not the number of jobs you create, for God's sake. If you have enough jobs for your people, you do not need to have a high rate of job creation- people are not insane. So the relevant indicator, which he did not talk about, is the level of unemployment. It is the level of unemployment that is the meaningful thing for comparative purposes. If you consider immigration, if you consider the birth rate and if you consider the fact that there are indeed men and women in this country who want jobs, the task of the government is to create a sufficient number of jobs so that they can work, instead of winning a meaningless statistical battle by saying that we have created more jobs than another country which does not have the same number of immigrants and the same birth rate.
When the Prime Minister came to office in 1968 there was a 3.4 per cent unemployment rate. In September of 1978 the rate was 7.7 per cent, an increase of 600,000 in real numbers

in that decade. He left the impression that now we are doing much better than other countries in terms of real performance, not in terms of the average in the ten-year period. We are talking now about a government which brought down the throne speech and which has to accept responsibility for what it has done for four years and what it plans to do for the next year before it calls an election.
How does our rate of unemployment compare with that in other industrial countries? According to the last yearly average in 1977, the rate of unemployment in Japan stood at 2.1 per cent, in Germany at 3.5 per cent, in France at 5.2 per cent, in the U.S. at 7 per cent, in Italy at 7.2 per cent, and in Canada at 8.1 per cent. We are the worst of the lot in the average for 1977. But the Prime Minister did not mention that.
With regard to inflation levels he thought we were doing wonderfully. He did not tell us the current level in Switzerland, Japan or Germany, which are all doing much better than this country, and I can list many others.
As to redistribution of income, my God, I thought for a minute I was listening to Trotsky. This man who came to office in 1968, this man who alleges now that he is really concerned about the Tory housing policy because he wants to do something for the low income groups, this man who, in his combative style, maintains he is so deeply concerned about inequality, does not face the fact that after having been in office for ten years there is more inequality today than we had in 1968.

speechtext: Not true.

speechtext: It is true; check your figures.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext:
I listened for two hours-it is my turn now. If hon. members check the statistics in the past decade, they will find that the situation of the poor in this country has become marginally worse-not a great deal but marginally worse-not better. This man who talks about inequality has done nothing about it for ten years, and yet he berates the official opposition as if really he had been centrally concerned.
The Prime Minister talks about good housing, about housing starts, as if it were some miraculous, fantastic accomplishment. He said we have created more houses than countries like Norway, Belgium or Sweden. Again I repeat that they do not have immigrant societies, they do not have thousands of people coming in every year, and they do not need to renew their housing stock the way we need to.
If ever a man should turn his own distinction back upon himself, I say it is the Prime Minister. If he wants to talk about reason and intelligence as opposed to imagination, I say he has provided a lovely set of imaginative statistics that are designed to try to convince everyone. What did he say? He said at one point that "we are doing very well indeed". I say that if you select your data carefully, you can convince Liberal backbenchers who are looking for something to get them out of

their morass, but I tell you that he will not convince the ordinary person in this country.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
In the throne speech almost no attention was paid to what I think is the central issue, and that is the state of the Canadian economy. There are other matters too. It is correct, as the Prime Minister said and also as the Leader of the Opposition has said on other occasions, that you cannot separate national unity or the problem of our federal state from the state of the economy. But may I emphasize that the central concern is the economy. The central way, but not the exclusive way, of dealing with national unity also is economic.
What is the major economic dispute in this land right now? No one met that dispute head on. 1 should like to deal with it in terms of the Prime Minister. Although my differences with the hon. Leader of the Opposition on principle are significant and real, it is the Prime Minister and the government of the day who are responsible for getting us out of our difficulties. What is the economic reality? As everyone knows, there are more than one million unemployed. The private sector is operating at 85 per cent capacity. In real terms the business sector has not indicated that it wants to invest more next year than this year. As I have said on other occasions, businessmen are not foolish or stupid. If they are operating at 15 per cent unused capacity, they will not change that now. They will not overexpand another 15 per cent or so.
If this is the reality, with our level of unemployment and the private sector not expanding, what should we be doing? For a minute I thought the Prime Minister was going to be serious instead of being polemical. He spoke about the level of government stimulus. Also he made an entirely misleading and facetious comparison with Saskatchewan. He said that the government is providing more stimulus than Saskatchewan in order to create jobs. Of course, what he did not mention was that the unemployment rate in Saskatchewan is 3.6 per cent. In the whole period he has been in government he has not achieved that level nationally. Of course, the level of stimulation must be much greater at the federal level. In managing a mixed economy with intelligence, Allan Blakeney in Saskatchewan has achieved virtually full employment. The Prime Minister should talk to him, in addition to Helmut Schmidt, if he wants lessons in economics.
The central reality in the land is whether we should adopt restraint as our principal economic policy-cutbacks, rollbacks, restraint. It all began with Sterling Lyon. I am not questioning the motives; I am questioning the policy argued by the official opposition. Now the Prime Minister, not having implemented his own promises for four years, since August 1 has been implementing the policies of the hon. Leader of the Opposition. Does that make economic sense? That is the question I want to raise and will attempt to answer.
We have a mixed economy. In my lifetime we have experienced, in Canada and throughout the world, the most
October 12, 1978

sustained period of economic growth in the history of man. From World War II to the present we have experienced the most sustained period of economic growth. Why is that? I ask the Prime Minister why that is so. The reason is that precisely during that period of time governments became involved in the economy. Because of the experience of the great depression, western economies all over the world, including the Government of Canada, have seen a central role to be played by governments in fiscal and monetary policies as well as seen the advantages of adopting an industrial strategy.
The argument made by the government in its Speech from the Throne and the argument made by the official opposition is that somehow we must cut back and restrain ourselves into prosperity. It is bad economics and worse social policy for this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It will not work. Under these circumstances we are saying that instead of cutbacks and layoffs, which would be the effect of a restraints program, of a further 100,000 Canadians by mindless and indiscriminate abolition of programs which are of benefit to Canadians, we need stimulation in the economy. We have said that taxes should be cut for ordinary people. There should be more cuts for lower income groups than high in order to provide stimulus. We have said that the federal sales tax should be cut by one-third to stimulate the manufacturing sector of the economy. Also we have said that there should be more public sector investment and that money should be put into needed energy projects, the housing sector for people who need homes, rapid transit facilities and grand national schemes. I will not go over the details of the package we proposed to the people of Canada any more precisely than I have already. This process would provide a real stimulus.
I say to the Prime Minister that the debt next year will go up approximately SI.5 billion. But if he looks at the level of private savings in this country, he will see that they are the highest since World War II. An elementary lesson in Keynesian economics would lead one to conclude that if we have a high level of saving in the private sector and by individuals, and the private business community is not expanding because of no demand, then the government should step in. If the Prime Minister looks at the record of Japan and the recent record of Germany over the last several years, their levels of debt for a number of years have exceeded ours because they stimulate at whatever level is needed in order to produce jobs and expand the economy.
Our proposal to create jobs for Canadians who want them, and to bring some real growth to the economy in the next decade, should start now with tax cuts for individuals, manufacturers and public sector investment. Yes, the debt will increase perhaps $1.5 billion next year; but according to our calculations, if the level of investment I have advocated outside the House is made, some 400,000 jobs would be created in the next two years, and in the next three years the national debt
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
would be reduced by some $6 billion to $7 billion. That is what serious economic policy should be all about at this time.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

AFTER RECESS
