subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne must be seen and understood in the context of the economic problems Canadians are now facing. What are those problems? We have one million unemployed. We have an industrial sector that is operating at only 85 per cent capacity, which means businessmen have decided not to expand. Businessmen are not foolish and are not going to take up another 15 per cent of unused capacity when they have more capacity than they now need. Also, and this is important and crucial to an industrial country, we have already lost some 15,000 jobs in the manufacturing sector in the past year.
What response has the government made? The Prime Minister for four years has been ignoring his own commitments and promises to the people of Canada, yet since August 1 he has been attempting to implement those of the Leader of the Official Opposition. This approach to a complex economy can be summed up as a policy that amounts to nothing more than a slogan; it is cutbacks, rollbacks and restraint. According to the Government of Canada we can now in 1978 restrain ourselves into prosperity. That is ludicrous in principle and it is harmful in its effects.
We recall that at the outset of economic difficulties during the time of the great depression the prime minister of the day applied the same policy. It did not work for R. B. Bennett in the 1930s and it will not work for Pierre Elliott Trudeau and the people of Canada in the 1970s. We do not have to go back to the 1930s because, unfortunately, we have a good example already before us of what happens when you apply an across the board restraint and cutback policy.
Not long ago in the province of Manitoba a Conservative government was elected principally on that policy, and it applied it. According to the unemployment statistics which came out earlier this week, the province of Manitoba with that cutback philosophy, which has now been taken over by the Liberals and preached by the Leader of the Opposition, experienced in one year an increase of 35 per cent. The rate of increase in unemployment in the province of Manitoba over the past year was four times the rate of increase in the country as a whole. That is the kind of result you get when you adopt an economic policy that amounts simply to cutbacks.



October 12, 1978
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
At the national level, when we heard from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) some six weeks ago that they were going to apply a program that was described in broader detail in the throne speech last night, we calculated that the effect on the economy as a whole would be a net loss of some 100,000 jobs.
I questioned the Prime Minister about that the other day. I asked whether he would confirm that an assessment within the Department of Finance had yielded that expectation. As usual, he was evasive and did not answer. Today in the city of Ottawa a private economic consulting firm made a report which pointed out that with the policy announced by the Government of Canada we would lose not 100,000 jobs, as we calculated, but some 94,000 jobs. That means more men and women will be collecting unemployment insurance and welfare instead of contributing in a positive way to the economic development of this country.
The President of the Treasury Board said in the House today that the federal government was really talking about man-hours and not people. Let me point out to him, and he ought to know, that already in the city of Ottawa over 1,700 civil servants have received their quit slips. They have been informed they are losing their jobs. These are not abstract statistics and not mere man-hours, these are men and women: some 362 in Statistics Canada, 250 in Public Works, 650 in National Health and Welfare and 500 in the Public Service Commission. Some 1,762 have already received notice that they will be unemployed. That is the consequence of what I think can only be described as an irresponsible and mindless economic policy. Whether this kind of program is implemented by a man named Trudeau, as prime minister, or by a man who would like to have that job, Joe Clark, makes no difference to the NDP all across Canada, and we will have nothing to do with it.
What do we propose to put in its place? I submit that what we want to do instead is not designed to create Utopia overnight and will not remove all aspects of inflation or completely obliterate unemployment within a year or two. What we propose is a policy designed to come to grips with the real world rather than some pseudo-fantasy created by the government and the official opposition.
What does it consist of? It consists of the kind of package that has worked so well in West Germany as applied by Helmut Schmidt where unemployment and inflation are at approximately 3 per cent. It has worked very well in Japan where they have unemployment and inflation around the same level. Both of those countries approached the problems of their economies not by denigrating the public sector, but by seeing in a modern economy that it plays an integral and fundamental role in the development process.
So what do we say? If you have manufacturing which is operating at only 85 per cent capacity when you want men and women to be employed on those unused machines, we say reduce the federal manufacturers sales tax by one-third. We

have recommended that, and we calculate that if it is done it would inject approximately $1.5 billion of stimulus into the economy, producing some 75,000 jobs-jobs in the manufacturing sector that would benefit those in the electrical industry in Ontario, those who are producing wood products in British Columbia, those working in the shoe industry in the province of Quebec; in short, Canadians in every part of our land who are involved in manufacturing.
Secondly, we would recommend that men and women who are not employed but have sufficient income to be paying income tax be given an income tax reduction. But unlike the other parties, we say let us give a greater tax reduction to those with the lowest income; starting at the lowest level, a $400 tax cut and diminishing the higher up the income tax scale you go, finally fading out entirely at the very rich level. I include in this category members of parliament whose incomes do not warrant a tax cut. We recommend a one and a half billion dollar tax cut of that kind. The net effect we calculate would produce some 125,000 jobs.
The third element of our proposal at this time, which so clearly distinguishes us from the Conservative party and the government of the day, is that we recommend, at a time when the private sector is not investing-because businessmen are not foolish-that we inject public capital to stimulate the economy. We recommend public sector investment of $1.7 billion.
Where would this money go, Mr. Speaker? We say that we need rapid transit facilities in downtown Toronto, which the government promised some time ago. We would expand these public transit facilities thereby putting unemployed construction workers in Toronto to work. We recommend that the Hall royal commission report that the government has sat on for so long should be implemented. If it were implemented, we would not only be meeting the needs of farmers in the prairies who want improved grain handling facilities to get their wheat to export markets, but we would also be providing jobs in Nova Scotia where they make the rails and railroad cars. Instead of a 30 per cent unemployment level in Cape Breton, perhaps it would be cut in half.
With that kind of package-a personal income tax cut, a federal manufacturers sales tax cut and public sector investment-we would over a two-year period create some 400,000 jobs. This would begin to turn things around in this country in the way that the people of our land desperately desire and expect politicians who assume their responsibilities to act. These are the things which are needed right now in the short run.
Beyond the short run requirements that ought to be acted upon for the people of Canada, we must give now-and it ought to have been included in the throne speech-some serious commitment to a long-range industrial strategy. The issue is not the bogus one the two old line parties would like to con the people of Canada into believing, that it is either small government or big government. The issue is effective government. Are we going to at long last have effective government leadership in this country?
October 12, 1978

We say we need it. The NDP say we should be doing here what other industrial countries have done, what Japan did after World War II when they decided that they would become the leaders of the world in the electronics industry. They began to put their research and development money into that field, and there was co-ordinated government leadership with the private sector to make sure that money went into research and development. My party says let us start doing that long-range planning now in our country.
There are, for example, three important sectors; food, housing and transportation. Eighty per cent of Canadian expenditures are in these three sectors. Let us improve them. Let us take our food industry and make it one of the most productive and efficient industries in the world, not only to meet Canadian needs but to enable us to get into the export business. We could be developing our food processing industry abroad. There is the example in the Atlantic provinces of the fisheries industry in Newfoundland, one of the last great fisheries in the world. We should be expanding it with our 200-mile limit. We could do for fishermen what we did for our farmers many years ago.
We set up the Wheat Board for our farmers. It went into the world markets and sold wheat for Canadian farmers to Asia and Europe, and as a result our farmers are among the best paid in the world. If there was a little initiative coming from this government, we could do the same for fishermen on the east coast and on the west coast. We could be expanding sales. We have an 85-cent dollar. Let us use that to take the opportunity to get into new markets and lay the foundation for more jobs. That way the province of Newfoundland-and I do not exaggerate-within a matter of years could be self-sustaining in the fishing industry and men and women there would be collecting pay instead of handouts or unemployment insurance. That is what the people of Newfoundland and the rest of Canada as well want.
The same could be said for development in housing and transportation. But then there are certain more crucial, fundamental sectors. I say to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), who is here tonight and who should know from his own responsibilities within his department, that there are certain aspects of Canadian industry which are second to none in the world, and if we had the right kind of development at this time we could be world leaders in terms of sales, thereby providing thousands of Canadians with jobs. In this context I think particularly of our computer industry, the energy development field which includes hydro and nuclear facility developments abroad, and the plastics and food processing industries. However, we must begin now with concentration on and careful selection of certain sectors of this kind for development to provide continuing jobs in the future.
Above and beyond the selection of certain crucial areas for international development that could provide for continued and sustained jobs, there is a fundamental difference as well between members of my party and the other two parties on the question of resource development. We have said for years that
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
it is time we stopped exporting our raw materials and buying back finished products from other countries.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We should be exporting steel, not iron ore; plastics, not unprocessed gas and oil; wood and paper products, not raw pulp. The underlying assumption is industrial strategy at the national level. In every province where resources are the key, we must have a resource policy whereby Canadian resources are developed by Canadians for the benefit of Canadians. That is what it should be all about.
This approach at this time, a short-run program designed to provide some 400,000 jobs and get people off welfare and handouts, combined with a long-range strategy, is what we ought to have had in the throne speech instead of the cutback, restraint mentality which is essentially negative and which will eventually lead to fewer, not more, jobs.
In conclusion, in suggesting this course of action for the people of Canada on behalf of my colleagues and this party, I do not say it is perfect; I do not say all our difficulties are going to go away but I do say that it recognizes reality. It recognizes that we have a mixed economy; it recognizes that we cannot go back to some primal existence that did not work in the 1920s and 1930s in terms of economics. If implemented, if acted upon by this government even before they face the electorate in the next election, what it would do for young Canadians, for old Canadians, for men and women who want to work is restore a sense of optimism and confidence about this country.
Canadians of my generation were lucky in the main. We grew up in prosperous times. For the most part we had things better than our parents, better than the young people coming on the labour market now. I, as leader of the New Democratic Party of Canada, and all of my colleagues want desperately to create the possibilities for young Canadians that we had in our youth. That is why we are advocating the kind of policy that I have outlined tonight.
Because of these positive things that are not in the Speech from the Throne and which we think ought to be there, I should like to move an amendment to the motion proposed by the Leader of the Official Opposition. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and this House condemns the government for its lack of economic planning and an industrial strategy, as evidenced by its failure to make a commitment to stimulate economic growth by reducing the federal sales tax, by reducing personal income taxes on middle and lower income earners, and by embarking on a new program of public sector investment."

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The opening of the fourth session of the thirtieth legislature of Canada went rather smoothly compared to the big demonstrations of the past, and I am pleased about this. I think the

October 12, 1978
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
Canadian people in general prefer their elected representatives and their administrators to be less demonstrative and more efficient. Having said this, I want to congratulate Mr. Speaker for remaining in office, and I hope that under his guidance parliament will do an outstanding job and lead our country on the road to economic progress, harmony and social peace. I also want to congratulate the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) who remains Deputy Speaker and the hon. members who will still act as deputy chairmen of the committees. I also wish to welcome the young women who will be pages in this chamber from now on. This is a good initiative, and I am pleased about it.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to note that the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) and leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada is absent for health reasons. All hon. members will certainly agree with me that the hon. member for Roberval who has been sitting in this House for 16 years is a glutton for work and that his contribution to the business of the House has always been marked by an objectivity and a sincerity worthy of a good Canadian.
You will certainly notice that I do not have the advantage of having behind me many hon. members to show on television how hardworking we are, as is often the case on the government side. However, I am not here to win applause, but I want to thank my hon. colleagues opposite and other hon. members who were kind enough to applaud me when I was invited to take the floor by the Chair. It is a mark of good fellowship. It also shows, I hope, that we are all working together in the best interests of the country. After all, Mr. Speaker, what is most important is to be here to fulfil my duties, to represent the people which sent me to parliament, to represent also the country as a whole, to speak on behalf of those who cannot come here to speak for themselves, that is the little people, the workers, the small businessmen, the small merchants, the farmers, the professionals, in other words, the entire population. So, let us forget about television for the moment and try to be efficient.
Mr. Speaker, I must heartily congratulate the sponsor and seconder of this motion who did their duty. I listened to their statements and I believe that the government should take heed of the suggestions put forward, especially with regard to the well-being of our families and senior citizens. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made similar remarks in his speech this afternoon. That means that we all wish for the well-being of our families, that we all want to ensure that our senior citizens have a well-deserved security and that it is up to parliament to guarantee them that security.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne contains the same ideas so often expressed on such occasions. And it is a good thing, because so long as problems remain unsolved, they have to appear on the order of business of the Parliament of

Canada. To repeat the same things over and over again is not a bad thing; on the contrary, I think it is a good thing, since it is to show confidence in the principles that prompt individuals or political parties in the pursuit of their objectives. Does not God himself set the example by making the sun rise every morning? And when skies are grey, are we not sad because we cannot see it rise? So, why not imitate our Creator?
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne stresses the problems caused by inflation, the resulting unemployment and Canadian unity which is going through a crisis which threatens the very existence of Canada. The majority party in the House, or at least its leaders, are aware of the seriousness of the situation, of the disorder in our economic system which brings about inflation and thus forces a great many workers into unemployment against their will.
Some will argue that some are wilfully unemployed and refuse to work. Let us say that these are exceptional cases. We must not generalize. Each week, people come and ask me to help them find a job. It is the same in our manpower centres, at any rate those in my area. Many workers go there and ask our employment officers to help them find work. In spite of their goodwill, those officers find it impossible to find a job for them.
Mr. Speaker, a wise judge has said at the hearing of an employment insurance case that you cannot expect anyone to look for something which does not exist. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that you cannot find a thing which is just not there and this is exactly what is happening now in our country as workers are looking for jobs which are not available. I have already said to the House that no good mother would send her jobless son, whom she is supporting, out to pick strawberries in October by threatening to starve him, if he does not. Everybody knows that strawberries don't grow in October. Even if the boy did try, surely he would not find any. These would be conditions impossible to meet.
A proverb says that you cannot teach an old dog new tricks. By the same token, nobody will convince me that our whole work force has suddenly turned lazy. I heard that argument during the depression years, 1929-1939, and hon. members of my own age may recall such remarks about the unemployed. People who had jobs and financial security would somehow claim that if the unemployed and the poor were in that condition, it was all of their own doing.
Mr. Speaker, as it turned out, the opposite was true. As soon as the leaders of that time, who were puppets of big business and big financial interests, declared World War II, the unemployed who were supposed to be heartless loafers answering the call of the authorities, enlisted in the Canadian army or applied for jobs in ammunition plants, to supply the European war sites. Others answered the call as farm hands. As former chairman of an intensive production committee and as a good Canadian, I wished to take part in my country's war effort to save our freedoms, so I remember appealing to my fellow
October 12, 1978

countrymen for more production to feed our armed Forces, and ammunition plant workers. That call was met generously. Those so-called lazy people became model labourers, so much so that government officials boasted about our workmen's efficiency and outstanding performance both in factories and on the battlefields.
Mr. Speaker, the same causes will have the same effects. We are witnessing a flash-back to the dirty thirties and were it not for our Canadian social security programs, the current economic depression would have still more serious consequences than at that time, because prices are now higher and the cost of living has reached an all-time high. Some cabinet members are aware of that serious problem and have the courage to speak out. I am referring to the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), the hon. member for Saint-Michel, who is quoted as making a sensational statement in Langford Mills. Her comments were reported in Le Droit on May 29, 1978, and I quote:
Two million children live in families whose income is insufficient to meet their needs, stated Miss Monique Begin, Minister of National Health and Welfare, speaking over the weekend to the national council of the Young Men's Christian Association.
Miss Begin said that in the case of at least 600,000 workers' families, two-thirds of the income is spent on food, clothing and lodging-
-but what is left for the other things?
The share of income in the hands of our poor families has changed very little since the end of the Second World War, she said.
Yet, this afternoon, I heard statements that totally contradict the thoughts of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
This would lead us to believe that despite their good intentions, the most fortunate Canadians have found a way of pulling out of the recessions on the backs of the poor.
This afternoon, the right hon. Prime Minister said that his government would strive above all to have the neediest share in the great wealth of this country; I feel he is right and, on that score, I am of those who are ready to help him, because, indeed, where our poorest families are concerned, we often seek out in those families the persons who are the most devoted to society, who at times make a career of it in our society.
Miss Begin ended her speech on these words:
-our economic system must be changed to encourage and not discourage work. Our economic system serves millions of Canadians poorly.
Mr. Speaker, may I, in passing, congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare for introducing a measure to improve the lot of our neediest families through higher family allowances. Yet, I am one of those who are in favour of universal family allowances. I do not think that the wife of a doctor who earns $100,000 a year should be penalized by receiving lower allowances than the wife of a labourer, because in my opinion motherhood cannot be assessed in dollars. I feel
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
that we should have universal family allowances and those who earn higher incomes should automatically, as in the case of old age security, pay taxes and definitely reimburse the treasury.
Mr. Speaker, I must express my gratitude on behalf of the senior citizens who will receive an increased pension supplement of $20. I would also like to express the wish that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will introduce some amendment to the legislation providing the payment of a pension or a supplement to an individual who has not yet reached 65 years of age but whose spouse is 65 years old or over.
Mr. Speaker, many of my constituents are suffering as a result of that fact. Following the death of the older spouse, the survivor who has not yet reached 65 is no longer entitled to a pension. It is quite distressing. I think we should all agree in the House that when an individual has received that pension or a supplement, he should still get it even after the death of his spouse. I am convinced that Canada will not be on the verge of bankruptcy for that reason and the victims could thus avoid some very serious problems.
Mr. Speaker, all types of productive power can meet the needs of all human beings living on this planet. God would not be the Almighty Being of infinite wisdom in whom I believe with all my heart if He would allow more human beings to be born on this planet than there are goods to meet the material and intellectual needs of everyone. A good father would not do this, hence our Father in His infinite wisdom cannot let this happen. If there are thousands of people on our planet in dire poverty, it is not because of a shortage of goods, but rather because of the lack of adequate means of distribution and purchasing power.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that all will agree that during the last session both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) said that generally we must strive to raise the purchasing power of the entire population, of low wage earners, for the benefit of the whole country.
Mr. Speaker, in early September I was in Africa as a member of a delegation of the Canadian parliament. I attended all sittings of the commission I belonged to with other Canadian parliamentarians from whatever parliament they were members of. In the course of our proceedings I heard a member from Zaire deplore the fact that a lack of paper prevents his country from getting enough books printed to meet the needs of the population and this is why thousands of Zairians remain ignorant because they cannot learn how to read and write-two indispensable tools which enable each individual to get an education and learn what is going on around the world. Anyone can get an education with these two tools if he has the willpower and the desire to do his own investigations and to learn more. As a member of the Canadian parliamentary delegation I made myself a duty to intervene to demonstrate that men and not God are responsible for such a state of things. Zairians have no paper for printing books to

October 12, 1978
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
educate their people while in Canada, in my province, in my own riding of Bellechasse hundreds of wood producers have worked hard to cut wood and pile it on the public road for shipment to the paper mill and yet they are unable to sell it so it will be shipped to its destination. Paper mills are closing their doors in several communities of our country especially in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, that is an example of human foolishness. On the one hand workers have produced pulp for the production of newsprint or other products and they cannot sell it in order to get their reward for their toil. On the other hand there are nations which cannot get the necessary paper used to produce schoolbooks to ensure the education their citizens are entitled to get as human beings. This is only one example of a bed distribution of goods due to the stupidity of an economic system which is not motivated, or rather which is motivated solely by profit and not by distributive justice. On the American continent, our workers and our industries are faced with over-production, yet elsewhere on other continents, especially in Africa, people are doomed to starvation. Elowever, the situation is no longer what it used to be several centuries ago. The means of communications and transportation of products are very efficient and would be even more so if those who have the monopoly of finance allowed our factories and our plants to build ships, trucks, planes and produce them in sufficient number to ensure the distribution of the goods so produced thereby satisfying the essential needs of human beings throughout the world.
We have in Canada, and specifically in Quebec, shipyards which have been operating at a snail's pace for many months, and skilled workers who are laid off because of lack of contracts to build ships which could transport Canadian products throughout the world and improve our trade balance. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) has repeatedly stated in the House that important shipbuilding contracts had been authorized, so what are we waiting for to execute them, to give work to our employees, our workers, so as not to be caught by surprise by a world war which could happen any day, as was the case in 1939. If we let our shipyards-and what I am about to say is extremely serious-deteriorate because of lack of contracts, we will one day find ourselves in an embarrassing situation. I think that for the welfare of Canadian industry, the cabinet should do its utmost to maintain our shipyards in operation, because a shipyard must always be working to stay abreast and maintain its expertise, that is to stay up to date.
I hope the government will take the necessary steps to reassure the shipbuilding industry and realize that we should keep that industry afloat to keep our expertise in Canada. That is why I say our interests dictate that we build up a shipping industry, which will enable us to face any eventuality and meet our responsibilities as a member of NATO.

As far as economic incentives and the fight against inflation and unemployment are concerned, Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne does not propose anything of any value unless I did not understand its full meaning. Are we to believe that the government no longer trusts its own programs, namely Canada Works, and could it be why the moneys previously earmarked for that program have been considerably reduced? I thought, Mr. Speaker, the aim of the program was to create jobs and make it possible for communities to carry out essential public projects.
Last Sunday, October 8, I attended the opening of a community centre at Saint-Nazaire, a town in my riding. The organizers of that project had applied for a grant under the Canada Works program, I had recommended the project to the minister and it had been accepted. On behalf of the people of Saint-Nazaire and my own, I thank the minister for the $48,000 grant which was provided for the completion of that project. To my great surprise, and I would like to call the attention of members of the cabinet to that fact, Mr. Speaker, although that centre cost $120,000, only $16,000 is still due, the difference between the $48,000 federal grant and $120,000 has been covered by the local residents who certainly deserve full credit. Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we heard about voluntary work. In the case that I mentioned, I believe that there was voluntary action and that the people involved wanted to make a common effort to reach a certain objective.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the result of a good program when it is well applied, well administered and able to stimulate the economy. This is why I say that in view of the present economic difficulties, the government should increase the funds of the Canada Works program while being careful in selecting the projects submitted to prevent wasting public funds. It is always essential to have some control. But in the case that I have mentioned, I can assure you that I was happy to be able to help to inaugurate this community centre in a small town of 450 people. This is extraordinary. It is the proof that there are people who really want to survive and ensure the survival of their village.
1 also submit that it would be a good thing to review the implementation standards of this program so as to be able to help when need be in implementing a project which has gone through a first stage and which could survive if the public authorities made a small effort. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the employees of the Department of Employment cannot always understand the needs of the community and the objectives of a project, and on the basis of the standards which have been set, they are forced to apply the legislation and the regulations as they are told without taking into account the fact that life must go on and that, with a little help, a business can eventually provide work for the community and provide for essential needs which must be met at all levels.
October 12, 1978

I therefore wish, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the mayor of the municipality, Mr. Claude Lachance, a young man full of ambition and courage, along with all his colleagues and the residents who participated financially and through their voluntary services, again a good example for our youth. Mr. Speaker, you cannot put a price to such a thing as giving a good example to those who watch you, giving them the wish for a better life, giving them the courage to use their energy to participate with their follow citizens in the development of their environment. I believe that when such things occur, we must talk about them so that others may do the same.
Mir. Deputy Speaker: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired. I am convinced that if he asks for the unanimous consent of the House, he will be allowed to complete his remarks. Is there unanimous consent in the House to let the hon. member complete his remarks?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, for your help in asking for consent on my behalf. 1 am thankful to you and also to all my colleagues for their generosity. Frankly, I would not want to abuse, I will try to be brief, but I still have a few ideas which I would like to express and which should help us all, I hope, to do something really worthwhile for our country.
In continuing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would not want to forget mentioning that in the interests of the Canadian people it is urgent that the government increase its help to small and medium businesses for they provide 60 per cent of all jobs in Canada. These businesses might go bankrupt by competition from large corporations and from multinational companies which unfortunately secure most of the government financial assistance. Mr. Speaker, it is an area on which I draw once again the attention of the government so proper care will be given to the distribution of government funds for industrial development so small and medium-sized businesses will have their share of the pie because those small and medium-sized businesses are operating mostly in rural areas and small villages while large corporations and large multinationals are working in large centres where they have all the economic advantages of transportation and communications they can hope for.
Mr. Speaker, small businesses are an important link in the Canadian economy. While serving the consumer they meet the needs of other small and large businesses. Although they cannot match the variety or volume of production of large businesses they still remain competitive from the point of view of prices, service, geographical location, presence in specific markets. According to the statistics, the number of small businesses in Canada varies between 800,000 and 900,000, about 90 per cent of all businesses. I, for one, attach a lot of
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
importance to these kinds of businesses which are sort of a rampart for the safeguard of private enterprise. That is why I suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) that he give small businesses additional tax rebates to allow them to survive and run at full capacity.
As we were coming back from Africa, Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I were exchanging points of view on what we had seen in those countries and what we had come to realize during the parliamentarians' conference. Then a colleague said that if we let farm producers produce what they can-and the same thing goes for the industrial sector-there would be no unsatisfied needs in the world and he said the problem was with means of distribution, not means of production. That colleague is a member of this parliament. I am sure he will support what I say when the time comes and take it upon himself to exert pressures so we can improve the system of distribution that could help solve a lot of problems.
Mr. Real Caouette, who was for many years the leader of my party and a member of this House-I refer to him with some emotion and everybody has recognized he was a great Canadian-explained often in this House the causes of that failure of our system in the distribution area in advocating measures like granting to the Bank of Canada more power to mint the nation's credit, the distribution of a national dividend to every Canadian, and a discount on Canadian products in order to increase the consumers' purchasing power and permit them to consume according to their needs to stimulate the economy of our country. I remember those words, and I am always faithful to that philosophy. That is why I recall his memory, and that is why I make a point of keeping in the same vein in order that we succeed in getting these changes we need.
As for what is contained in the Speech from the Throne about the Canadian constitution, Mr. Speaker, it is a general summary of what has often been stated by the Prime Minister. Again this afternoon we heard that policy, the statement of these principles, and I for one am glad to hear in the Speech from the Throne that another legislation will be introduced during this session as a replacement for Bill C-60 with some improvements I am anxious to know.
Mr. Speaker, I already have had the opportunity to express in the House my opinion on the serious matter during a debate on a motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on July 6, 1977. At that time I was hoping that parliament would review the work of the Senate committee which was appointed in 1970 to undertake a comprehensive study of the whole issue and which presented its report on March 16, 1972. And I think that if the recommendations contained in that report had been followed since 1972 we would have made much progress and we would be close to reaching an agreement on a new constitution, a truly Canadian constitution made by Canadians for Canadians.

October 12, 1978
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
I hope that some day this will be achieved and that following the adoption of that new constitution by the provinces and the Canadian parliament it will be submitted to the approval of all Canadians by way of a referendum. Our country will be given a fifth constitution, but it will be the first time in our history that it will be subject to approval by the people and I think that after its adoption a copy of the constitution should be given to every Canadian who should be encouraged to consider it as a credo for Canadians and to live by it and I think it is only under this condition that we shall have harmony in our country.
I say that my party agreed with the constitution. During a national assembly every issue has been considered and we should clearly establish that we are in a Christian country. We should first establish our faith in God. We should establish the rights and obligations of the individual as a human being, the rights and responsibilities of the family, the basis of our society, the rights and responsibilities of provincial governments and the federal government. If all those responsibilities and rights were established clearly it would put an end to those useless discussions on the constitution and as Canadians of whatever ethnic origin we might work more and make every effort to build and develop our country further.
We are now divided. Each side tries to pull harder than the other and we do not progress too fast. Economic problems are increasing dissatisfaction is growing and this has given rise to a critical situation which is of great concern to me. As a Canadian citizen, Mr. Speaker, I would like all members of parliament as well as members of provincial legislatures and those who are interested in solving that problem, the leaders of intermediate bodies, to make their contribution and enable us to draw up a Canadian constitution of which every Canadian would be proud.
Mr. Speaker, if we want to live harmoniously in Canada, that is what we must do. Those are the views which I cherish very deeply and after travelling throughout the country and having taken the views of the residents of other provinces, when we speak as gentlemen and as Canadians we arrive at that conclusion.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that as long as the provinces will be forced to beg the federal treasury for revenues they will complain about the invasion of the federal government in areas which are under provincial jurisdiction, and that is the main cause of the division we are experiencing in this country. I would like to remind my colleagues of two very real experiences I lived, one in 1935 and the other in 1940, but I will talk about them on another occasion in order not to abuse the kindness of the House.
Mr. Speaker, as far as Canadian harmony is concerned, if we want to achieve our objectives, we will have to change- and I stress this-our system of financing the public sector, a burden which is becoming heavier every day, to wit the 78-79 budget whereby Canadians will have to pay $6.5 billion in

interests on the public debt, which is $1.65 million more than last year. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the national debt increases by $31 million each day, which is $11.5 billion over the current fiscal year. These are figures which Canadians must know and about which we should think very seriously. The government anticipates cuts in various areas but it fails to take the means to alleviate the burden of interests. Mr. Speaker, one of the way for the government to relieve the burden of debts and interests would be to amend the legislation on the Bank of Canada so that it be permitted to generate all the money supply the country needs. As it is, it generates only 8 per cent of it, 92 per cent being created by chartered banks. It should be the other way around.
Mr. Speaker, if the Bank of Canada is authorized to create 8 per cent of the money supply and if we use it with great confidence, why would it not be authorized to create 92 per cent of it? It is not normal that a public service as necessary as a monetary system be left into the hands of institutions whose first purpose is to make profits without considering the services and the primary function of a monetary system. Governments are at the mercy of those financial institutions, and I have here, Mr. Speaker, two copies of a magazine called Le Nouvel Informateur. I came across this publication by pure chance when 1 was on a plane coming back from Africa. This issue is very recent as it was published in September and it contains a description of the serious investigation made by a Frenchman, Philippe Simoneau, on the powers of bankers and how they use them. I invite my colleagues in the House to read it so that, when we consider the bill which was numbered 57 during the last session and which concerns the Bank Act revision, they will be able to contribute intelligently to the study of this bill and the amendments that will have to be made.
Mr. Speaker, in closing I would like to say that when we make such proposals there are always jokers to say that we want to implement a system of funny money in Canada. To these people I would like to ask if the tragic monetary system that we are now using is acceptable in view of the present results. Mr. Speaker, this does not shock me. The same things were said 38 years ago about the proposals of the Social Credit, and 1 would like to quote an editorial written by a man whom many people knew and who was the head of two important daily newspapers, Le Soleil of Quebec city and L'Action catholique, and who moreover is the father-in-law of Quebec Premier Rene Levesque. I am talking about Mr. Eugene L'Heureux. Here is what he said:
After ridiculing Social Credit like so many others, we are now able to look objectively at this monetary doctrine as we believe that it deserves to be studied in view of the present serious circumstances.
That was 40 years ago, but it is still true today, and I quote:
That is why we extend our heartfelt congratulations to those who take the trouble of investigating whether or not implementing certain Social Credit principles could help solve the ever-growing problems that classical economic schools of thought cannot resolve.
October 12, 1978

The situation has not changed today.
However, we think that one should think twice before totally rejecting this monetary doctrine without submitting it to a test as it is the only one so far that advocates a set of positive remedies to the problems brought about by the big financial interests that control the world.
It is quite possible that the solutions or part of the solutions suggested by the Socreds will prove inadequate. We hope that Social Credit opponents-who are just as convinced as we are that big money circles are responsible for the present crisis-will in their turn advocate systematic solutions and not only casual, inconsistent remedies devised only to poke fun at the Socreds.
Usually that is what they do, just for the fun of it. They cast aside our philosophy but they are not able to give us good reasons for it.
No one intelligent and honest really believes that the economic situation could go on worsening as has been the case for the last ten years without impunity and despite the bankers' optimistic hanky panky.
This afternoon the Prime Minister was quoting a banker, Mr. McLaughlin, who was just that type of optimist. Some hanky panky is pessimistic and indeed I read last year some books which were rather gloomy.
Let us hope that our fears will not be justified. But as much as the so-called utopian theories we fear the probable consequences of the lack of new ideas in the economic field and the passivity of our leaders.
As spectator interested in this human drama, neither for nor against social credit-
-he is objective, he does not suffer from tunnel vision.
-we admit that one can be against social credit-
So do I. Not just for the sake of it but as long as it is not a combat based on lies and derision. These accusations must be founded on something positive.
-on the condition that one comes up with something better to replace the social credit doctrine.
Clearly the world needs an economic revival.
It is the same thing today. I continue quoting:
-if social credit cannot provide the driving force let us propose a better medicine. We do not favour social credit all that much.
Neither do I and if some have better measures, let them bring them forward and I will support them.
It is time that the democratically elected people stop playing into the hands of high finance, directing all their efforts towards the consumption of means advocated by such and such group in order to insure their economic dictatorship.
And I will end now with these words:
This narrow negative work which could not serve better those who exploit the rest of the world probably holds in store nasty days for our society. We would like to stave off this tragic outcome.
And yet this was written 40 years ago!
We do not care whether social credit succeeds or not but the necessity, the urgency to do something to prevent monetary capital from prevailing over human capital cannot leave us indifferent.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with those words but I do not agree that government authorities should take more interest in and give more attention to the monetary capital which is soulless and lifeless, over the interest of human capital which repre-
The Address-Mr. Francis
sents life, which is the greatest wealth that God has given to mankind.
Mr. Speaker, once again I would like to thank my colleagues. I had a message to deliver and as spokesman for my party I had to deliver a more elaborate message, and I must thank my colleagues for understanding this important responsibility. I want to assure the House and all my colleagues of all my co-operation, because if there are more viable solutions to this debt problem, this situation where the dollar is overriding the importance of human capital, I am always ready to lend my support, even if that means working 24 hours a day.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the members for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) and for Verdun (Mr. Savard) who delivered such good speeches yesterday afternoon in the House. I intend tonight to deal with some problems of government policy, especially as they concern the national capital region and the public service.

When I was a student at university, we talked about the hungry thirties, which were followed by the frightened forties and the fabulous fifties. But what happened to the economy of our country and the western world in the sixties and the early seventies surpassed everything for which we could have hoped. In this period things got out of line. As far as Canada is concerned, we are now suffering the consequences of the maladjustments which crept into our economy. Our wage rates became higher than those of our trading partners. Our productivity did not keep pace. We lived high on the hog and now Canada, along with other nations of the western world, has to make some very painful adjustments.
The economic medicine which is prescribed is not popular. It is not the kind of thing which enhances an elected government in a democratic society. As a member from the national capital region, I feel every day the consequences of the policy which was described in the Speech from the Throne- restraint-and I am sure members of every other party represented in this House do also.
This afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) very well pointed out that the room within the federal budget for reduction in government expenditures, a policy which seems to be generally accepted as the kind of medicine we must face now, can only be applied in very restricted areas of the federal budget. We cannot reduce the statutory commitment for old age security. We cannot reduce interest payments on federal debt. We cannot reduce the money that must be paid to the provinces to support the cost of hospital and health insurance and so on. However, in areas in which federal services are rendered, whether it is national defence, whether it is housing, whether it is the services of the Departments of National Health and Welfare or Public Works, the federal government can apply its economy measures.

October 12, 1978
The Address-Mr. Francis
Those of us who are representing areas very heavily populated by public servants have the responsibility of saying to the people we represent: "You must by the very facts of life reflect national decisions and the national will. As your representative, I will do my very best to see that the policies are applied as fairly as I know how, but I will not deceive you, nor will I say things which are in themselves all things to all people, avoiding the hard facts and the tough decisions that have to be made".
The government has proposed cuts that involve some 5,000 indicated positions in a federal service of 300,000. I say "indicated positions"; they are not all filled. It is hard to say, but perhaps 3,500 of those will involve positions that are actually filled and will probably be declared redundant in the process of the examination of which functions the government is no longer going to perform. I choose my words carefully here, Mr. Speaker. I say "of which functions the government is no longer going to perform".
I have received calls, as have other people, from long-term civil servants. As an example, I received a call from an employee of the department of health who has been working for many years on the hazards of asbestos dust to health and is being laid off. I have received calls from people who have served in the public works testing laboratory conducting experiments over a long period of time and are being laid off.
I look at my colleagues around me and know they can multiply the examples that can be cited. The policy of the government will be pursued through attrition as much as possible, and through transfers as much as possible, but there inevitably will be some positions declared redundant, in respect of which the incumbents will not be able to find employment in the public service itself.
The Public Service Commission has a priority program of reassigning, and every facility will be offered within the public service to see what kind of additional posts can be found. The problem here has been complicated by the government's policy of decentralization, a policy which was applauded by every other party in this House of Commons. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) was elected officially by espousing decentralization. I remember the plea by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) of the NDP for more government services in his own backyard. Every party in this House has endorsed decentralization as an instrument of national unity. That has complicated the difficulty which public servants find now in searching for posts which are not filled and for which they would be qualified.
I note that the policy of decentralization by the Government of Canada has run into a snag which has very seriously delayed it. The province of Quebec has refused to guarantee the rights of the sons and daughters of public servants moved to that province to schooling in the language of their choice. The Government of Canada, through the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), has said that public servants will not be moved if the government of that province is not

prepared to guarantee those rights. I note some members on the other side are laughing a bit about this. I personally find this a very serious and intense matter.
The first comment we have is this. The cuts in government expenditures which are part of the package of economic kmedicine will mean some layoffs, and this will hurt. We know that.
Another policy that is implicit in the medicine has regard to wage restraints in the public service. The Speech from the Throne says:
You will be asked to approve amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act to ensure that compensation in the federal public service remains in step with the private sector, and does not lead the way.
As the Prime Minister indicated this afternoon, this commitment came out of a federal-provincial conference of the heads of government in Canada, and at that conference, as the Leader of the Opposition so eloquently pointed out, the opposition parties were well represented by the heads of the provincial governments.
The commitment which was unanimously given to that conference and accepted was that there should be some kind of restraint in excessive wage demands in the public sector. As a result we had Bill C-28. In the form in which that bill was presented to this House 1 could not support it; nor could many of my colleagues on this side. A number of us worked during the summer, and we have made a number of suggestions. I cannot speak for others, but I will speak for myself. I believe the government will bring in a much better bill.
The bill as originally drafted would have given guidelines to arbitrators to bring down awards recognizing total compensation comparability. It did not talk about the option of conciliation, which is the second option available to staff associations in the public service. Adoption of Bill C-28 in the form in which it was presented to this House would, in my opinion, have forced every staff association to have chosen the strike route, and would have very seriously undermined arbitration, which most of us consider to be a more desirable way of settling disputes.
The bill had other defects. It did not recognize the inequality of pay for women which the private sector has very seriously embedded in it. The Human Rights Act would perhaps have overruled the original draft of those clauses in Bill C-28. Bill C-28 had a technical error in the assignment of duties to individuals as well as to positions.
When we talk about the private sector we must remember that there is not just a nice neat little package with the label on it "private sector". There are all kinds of employers in the private sector, good ones and bad ones. There are sweat shops and well paid positions. Which employers are you going to make the comparison with? And if the objective is comparison of the public service, it should be with more than the private sector. It should be a comparison with outside employment. For teachers that would mean the municipal school boards, and for our nurses it would mean municipal and provincially operated hospitals.
October 12, 1978

Those of us who have looked at the act feel that the legislation dealing with total compensation comparability has to be much more sophisticated. There are over 100 elements involved in pay. What is the monetary equivalent of the public servants' superannuation plan for the private sector in your comparison? Those of us who have looked at the act feel there has to be an agreement through the pay research bureau for a means of working out that kind of comparison in dollars and cents terms.
Therein lies the possibility of compromise and negotiation. If there is not agreement on the method of doing the calculations, there can be no agreement on anything else and the arbitrators will not get meaningful instructions. We say this kind of a package is acceptable in principle. We know there are some sections of the public service that are under-paid as well as some that are over-paid. In any organization with 300,000 men and women there are bound to be maladjustments, particularly if you are trying to make a rational standard of comparison in order to develop salary and wage scales that can be applied generally.
I feel confident that the new bill which is coming in will be a much more acceptable bill, a much more humane bill, and those of us who are supporting the government on this side are doing our very best to make it so.
I want to say something with regard to a problem in the national capital itself. The relocation of some offices across the river involved some difficulties which seems to have been worked out. Most of the public servants that I know are very pleased to have such excellent working conditions in the new structures. The difficulties of transportation, income tax deductions and parking have all been worked out. Parking problems are no worse there than in many other places. However, there are still problems that have resulted from this move concerning vacant office space in the national capital. This could have been avoided through better planning and anticipation. I am hoping that the municipalities will not suffer an abrupt loss in revenue they would have received otherwise by way of grants or in lieu of taxes, and that the government will see its way clear to some adjustments which the Minister of Finance in a conference meeting with the municipalities this spring so clearly promised.
On Monday there are going to be a few by-elections. There is going to be a by-election in the constituency of Ottawa Centre which is next to mine. At the reception last night a charming lady came up to me and said, "I hear there is going to be a by-election in your constituency." I assured her that I was still there and that that report was something like the report of Mark Twain's death, which was slightly exaggerated. However, the voters in the constituency of Ottawa Centre will have to make a choice on Monday.
Let us look at the position of the official opposition party in this House. Nobody could have put it more eloquently than the Prime Minister when he said: "The desire of the official opposition party is to do everything painlessly; 60,000 public
The Address-Mr. Francis
service jobs out of 300,000 are going to disappear and nobody is going to feel it." It reminds me of the old fable of the man with the sword who swung at somebody's head and the fellow said, "You missed", and he said, "No, just shake your head." The suggestion that this can be done by attrition is an insult of the intelligence of any student. The Government of Canada has indicated 5,000 positions will disappear. If it is difficult for hon. members on the other side to think that 5,000 positions will not be absorbed by attrition, how can they absorb 20,000 a year by attrition?
The Prime Minister pointed out that attrition occurs in the wrong places, that it does not come where you want it. The policy of the government was to determine that certain functions would no longer be performed which would then eliminate the jobs in those areas. The policy of the Tory party is to say through this magic word, attrition, so many people are going to retire and we are going to have a full freeze on hiring for three years. At the end of three years the public service will be just as efficient and all vacancies are going to be in the right places, the total payroll at the end of three years will be down by $1.2 billion, and public servants won't even feel it. I do not think that the public servants of this country are going to buy that for one minute.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext:
I hear some members on the other side saying something about pensions in the government service. I know there has been a great deal said about the public service superannuation plan. I placed some questions on the order paper, and I received my answers just yesterday. In the public service superannuation account there is in excess of $9 billion as of March 31. The rate of interest is approximately 7.8 per cent and approaching 8 per cent. It is a weighted formula related to the interest rates on new borrowings.
The last time the Minister of Finance went to borrow money he paid 9.5 per cent for 20-year Government of Canada debentures. So the interest rate will still be rising. Over $700 million per year is coming in by way of interest payments, and the disbursements for basic pensions and escalation are scarcely more than half that, maybe $370 million. Out of this some people have made a disastrous scenario, but it has not been the professional people, the actuaries such as the Tomenson-Alex-ander firm which people were so worried about. They said that if we left the fund alone and did nothing it would exceed $40 billion by the turn of the century and if you did nothing with it eventually go over one trillion dollars.
The fund was set up with interest rate earnings of 4 per cent, and interest rates are now approaching twice that. The Conservative candidate in Ottawa Centre was "Mr. Conference Board" who led the attacks on the escalation of public service pensions, stating along with the national citizens coalition that they would wreck the country.
I understand that the Tory candidate said today in an open line program that he really approves of the escalation of pensions. Well, Mr. Speaker, he sure kept that a secret and managed to unveil it at the last minute, just before going to the

October 12, 1978
The Address-Mr. Francis
polls on Monday in a civil service constituency. 1 raised the question with the voters, "Is this the man you want to represent you when it comes to negotiating on legislation affecting public service superannuation?" The Speech from the Throne said that it is coming, that we will have amendments to the Public Service Superannuation Act designed to ensure that public service pensions are in line with contributions.
I remember the statements of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that day in March when the President of the Treasury Board made his declaration on what government policy would be. He said at that time that there would be some changes, that the government was going to stop the nonsense of having everybody retire on December 31 to get their escalation, and that it was going slowly, in a year by year process, to raise the escalation from age 55 to 60, and every three years they would look at the fund to see how much money was in it. With a 9'A per cent interest rate in the last government bond issue, I am not worried about whether there will be enough money in the fund to pay for escalation.
I say to the people of Ottawa and to the public servants that the government put escalation according to cost of living on the books on a fully actuarially funded proposition, in a fund that is basically so over-funded that it is almost scandalous, rising at a rate of over one billion dollars a year. There is protection for the retired pubic servant to ensure that the cost of living will not slowly steal a little bit each year from the pension that he or she has to live on. I am proud to be a member of the party that legislated this.
I said that there was a choice the voters would have to make, and it is a very significant choice. I invite them to consider the issue of the cost of pensions. They say that there is a third choice, another candidate for the New Democratic Party in that riding. The program which that party is putting forward is one where they are also promising everything painlessly. They do not accept the analysis of our economy and/or the economic medicine that we prescribe.
The weakness of the New Democratic Party is its lack of discipline. I remember the last time we had a Post Office strike-Lord forbid that we have another like it. At that time the Liberal candidate for Ottawa Centre was the postmaster general. I remember the debate in which the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) got up and said of the postal workers' demand for a 40 per cent wage increase that they should get it. There was not one word of criticism in that debate of anything that the union asked for. I can remember when Joe Davidson said that the public be damned if the union did not get what they wanted. I can remember Joe Davidson coming before the committee of the House of Commons which was looking at the amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act and saying that our postal rate should be 25 cents a letter.
It was a joint committee which included the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and I am sure that he can confirm that what I said happened. Nobody from his party said one word of criticism. Nobody. If we have a problem with comparability today in the public service, if we have some areas that

are out of line, if we have some very aggressive unions abusing the right to strike-and I say that if post office workers go on strike again they are abusing the right to strike, testing the public and elected representatives-then the members of that party have some responsibility for the encouragement they have given, their failure to condemn and their failure to be responsible in the position they took. Again I say to the people who are going to have to vote-

speechtext: It is true the employer is pretty good there.

speechtext:
I am not defending everything as being perfect on one side or the other. I am saying we have a tough proposition before us and the people are going to have to make a choice. If we are facing a policy of restraint, if we are facing a policy of some rates of pay being out of line, then we must ask why it happened and who the people are who encouraged it to happen.
The Public Service of Canada is crying for certain things to be done. The public service will serve the public. They know they must respond to a national will. They ask that they be recognized when they do a job well. They ask that they have the dignity they feel they should possess as human beings because they do a job with pride and with decency. They are embarrassed when there is waste; they are embarrassed when things are not right. They want the Public Service Staff Relations Act amended, and amended in a humane way. They are going to remember who it was put collective bargaining on the books in the first instance.
I submit that the amendments this House will finally carry will be more in the spirit of the original legislation than in the spirit of Bill C-28. Public servants are going to remember that the Public Service Employment Act also calls for substantial revision. They will await the report of the D'Avignon special committee of inquiry, on which there is not only Mr. D'Avignon as chairman but Mr. Davidge representing the employees and Mr. Bruce Brittain representing the employer. They are going to remember that this government enacted legislation according the full cost of living escalation to their pensions.
