October 12, 1978

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleagues for that generous applause, which I know is heartfelt and appropriate under all circumstances. I want to spend the few moments I have this evening addressing some remarks to the Speech from the Throne specifically and to look at some of the reasons we are back in parliament rather unexpectedly.
Before doing that, however, I want to extend to the mover, the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni), and to the seconder my sincere congratulations for the manner in which they carried out this very traditional and important function. The hon. member for York South spoke with great ability, perception and grace. She had a most difficult function, defending the indefensible, and I give her full marks for the way in which she presented her speech and attempted to carry out this almost impossible task.
Today is what is known colloquially as leaders' day. This afternoon and this evening I have been contemplating what the effect might be on someone who came into this chamber, as they might, to observe the speeches made this afternoon, particularly as far as the two main speakers were concerned. I think it is fair to say, and I believe most members would agree, that if any person who was disinterested in the affairs of this House had come into the chamber this afternoon, he would have been under the impression that the Prime Minister was the person sitting directly in front of me-the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in actual fact-because he spent his whole time charting the course of action as he saw it that had to be taken regarding the important issues in the country at this time.
What did we have from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)? We had a speech that could only be assessed as a scandalous personal attack on the very constructive suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition. It was the kind of attack that might be considered appropriate for an opposition leader, but the tone was set by the Prime Minister for the way in which this government is going to look at things in this session. The Prime Minister came forward carping and criticizing what I consider to be the very responsible and constructive suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition.
If this is the kind of atmosphere that the so-called leader of our country is going to create in this institution, what kind of progress will we make in the days and weeks ahead? I have to commend my leader for the way in which he conducted himself at a time when we have no business being in this parliament, a time when we should at last be going to the people for a new mandate, for a new government.
I want to point out to hon. members opposite that a provincial election is taking place in Saskatchewan right now. Maybe the Prime Minister should observe what is going on there. The premier, who was embattled and felt considerable pressure with respect to his office, started his campaign with a serious and uncalled for attack on the leader of the Conservative party in that province. I anticipate as a result of this uncalled for and unsubstantiated attack that in Saskatchewan after October 18 another will be added to the ever-growing list of
The Address-Mr. Hnatyshyn
Conservative governments. There will be seven after October 18.
I want to consider why we are here, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister spoke today of leadership and the kind of qualities he thought, in all modesty, that he could present to this country. He has given us examples of that kind of leadership over the last few months. We have no business being here now. There is nothing in the Speech from the Throne that warrants this government continuing in office. Can anyone in this House seriously suggest that there is anything of substance in the Speech from the Throne that will deal with the issues in the country at the present time? Are any new initiatives of any consequence being taken by this government with respect to the economy? Are there any suggestions with respect to the great so-called issue of national unity in our country?
It is simply a rehash, sir, of helter skelter announcements made by the Prime Minister over the course of the last few months without consultation with members of his cabinet. Unilaterally, as is his custom, he came forward with suggestions he thought would be politically appealing at this time. Quite frankly, in my estimation these suggestions were ones that he felt were necessary in order to save his political scalp.
I was elected in 1974, along with the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Abbott). Those of us who were elected in 1974 may be people who are going to make history because of the fact that we may be in this parliament a sufficient number of years to qualify for a pension. The kind of leadership we have from this Prime Minister is the pre-empting of programs on national television. He has done this on two or three occasions. On each occasion the great announcement for the Canadian people who have been waiting for this television appearance is: "I am sorry, but I am the leader of the country and there will be no election".
I am reminded that over the course of the summer the Prime Minister went to Bonn for the summit meeting, along with other leaders of western countries. I could only come to the conclusion that while he was there he must have done some good. 1 think what he did for Canada was possibly sell his now patented speech to Mr. Callaghan, who gave a similar speech in England not too many weeks ago. The only accord that I have seen come out of the Bonn summit is to say that those who were involved in the deliberations possibly agreed that there would be no more elections.
Let us remember the Prime Minister has a basic contempt for this institution to the extent that he rarely, if ever, participates in the debates in this House. In fact during the time I have been here he has only been seen in debate on one occasion each year, and that is on the occasion of the Speech from the Throne debate. That is the way in which he regards the institution of parliament. That is the way this Prime Minister feels about obtaining advice from members of his own party, or indeed members of the opposition representing, as we do, every region and part of Canada.

October 12, 1978
The Address-Mr. Hnatyshyn
Undoubtedly members on his side of the House will be quick to point out that he comes in during the question period with his idea of answers to questions. But he is really setting a precedent as far as prime ministers are concerned, in terms of our parliamentary history, by the way in which he ignores and disregards this House. He does not participate in debates. He ignores members on his side, refusing as he does to take advice from them respecting the issues of the day.
It is no secret, and I know members on the other side will agree, that the Prime Minister is seeking less and less advice from caucus. Indeed, long ago he stopped taking advice from his cabinet. He has surrounded himself, and continues to do so, with a small clique of advisers in the Prime Minister's office. This is the ruling class in Canada today. This is the kind of participatory democracy we now have in Canada, participatory democracy, as we all recall, being promised by the Prime Minister at the time he started out in politics and at the time he started out as Prime Minister. Members on the government side know full well that if they want anything done, if they have anything to say or anything to ask for, they have to get permission and clearance and go through this clique of advisers to the Prime Minister.
I hope to demonstrate in the course of my remarks that the Prime Minister is withdrawing more and more from the traditional parliamentary system and proceeding into a system more akin to a presidential system, one where his word, and his word alone, his opinion and his opinion alone, are given consideration. The cabinet and his own parliamentary group are mere appendages to suit the convenience of the "philosopher king". 1 say "philosopher king" with the emphasis on the "king". The leadership given by this Prime Minister is the leadership of fear-fear of facing the electorate. That is the kind of leadership we have experienced. Notwithstanding his histrionics and rhetoric today and his attack on the suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition, one thing that has marked his particular time in office is that which demonstrates he is very wary and reluctant to face the electorate.
We are here for the purpose ostensibly of dealing with some of the great problems that we have. We are now faced with a Prime Minister who is more concerned with his own survival than he is with the real needs of our country. I say that more out of a sense of chagrin than a sense of criticism. If this Prime Minister really had the interests of Canada in his heart he would go to the people.
What we need now is not short-term policies put forward, of whatever type, but a fresh government with a fresh mandate. Anyone who has any concept of planning the economy and as well national unity would understand that a fresh government of whatever stripe after an election would have at least four years within which to put in reasoned and planned policies and programs that would be instituted over a period of time. Difficult decisions could be made because there would be a new mandate for the new government.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are about to rise. Therefore may I call it ten o'clock and continue my remarks tomorrow?
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE WITH PROVINCES
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I put a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) during question period today. I think it is important that all members of the public know where their political representatives stand on issues as important as unemployment insurance. I was somewhat reassured by the minister's reply. However, he did not address himself to that part of my question in which 1 asked for the tabling of any correspondence between the provincial premiers and himself. I want to have that information tabled, if it exists, in the interests of providing to Canadians the positions of the premiers.
It is well known that at the first ministers' conference last winter the premiers approached the conference with a very tough stand against increased government expenditure. It was a stand for cutting the fat and cutting back on employment by government, etc. I am not criticizing that stand at all, Mr. Speaker; there are obvious areas where cutbacks can and should be made. However, this is the time of elections in some parts of the country. The Tory premier of New Brunswick does not have much of a record of his own to run on, and to date he has been running on federal issues, issues which he does not seem to know much about. He forgets that over half of the money his government spends comes from the federal government. He did not talk about that during the campaign. He talked about false issues. From what was said by that government's representative at the conference with the Minister of Employment and Immigration yesterday, he does not know what the proposals with regard to unemployment insurance are all about.
The principle of unemployment insurance is extremely important. It is a principle to which this government is and must remain firmly committed. Other principles are involved which must not be violated. One of these is relatively new. In fact, it is only about 18 months since the principle of variation of benefits and, more particularly, qualifying periods in the Unemployment Insurance Act was brought in. Those regional variations must remain. In fact, there should be more of them. We must not carry on with this fetish that everything must be the same in all parts of the country, because the same conditions do not exist at any given time in all parts of the country. Therefore, we must protect and enhance the idea of regional variations. There are many changes that could be made in the Unemployment Insurance Act without reducing benefits to those who really need them.
October 12, 1978

There is something which must be said, and it cannot be emphasized too much. There are some abuses of the unemployment insurance scheme. However, all of those abuses are blamed on the employees. In many cases, the employer is as guilty as the employee. An employer too cowardly to write on a separation slip that an employee left without cause or was fired without cause is as guilty of ripping off the unemployment insurance scheme as the employee who takes the money.
I see no difference in the situation. However, it is always the employee who is villified by the critics of unemployment insurance.
One change that could be made in the program would be to write into the act very tough penalties for employers who falsify separation certificates. That would take away some of the stigma from those who, through no fault of their own, receive unemployment insurance benefits, benefits to which they have contributed.
This is not a welfare scheme as many people seem to think. No doubt there are those who try to use it as a welfare scheme, but it is not that. Those who draw unemployment insurance benefits have paid into the scheme for the benefits they are receiving. I do not pretend that they pay premiums equivalent to the benefits they receive. Many people pay premiums all their working lives and never receive any benefit except the termination benefit when they retire. It is important to remember that this is an insurance scheme.
It is essential that the information I asked for earlier today be made public so that people will know where their political representatives stand. Certain premiers could not then raise false issues, taking one stand at a conference at Ottawa and then taking the exactly opposite stand in their province because it is convenient to do so during an election campaign.

speakeroldname: Mr. Frank Maine (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this afternoon's question period the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) asked whether, in view of yesterday's
Adjournment Debate
press reports, the minister could confirm that all provincial premiers are opposed to changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act. I take it that the hon. member was referring to provincial ministers with manpower responsibilities because these press reports related to a federal-provincial conference which took place yesterday in Ottawa dealing with proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I am not aware that the subject of changes to the unemployment insurance program has been raised at the prime ministerial level in any of the provinces. I happened to be at the federal-provincial conference which took place yesterday, so I can assure the hon. member that I am in a position to set the record straight.
It is fair to say that there was a frank and open discussion about the changes which are being proposed and, as the minister himself indicated in the House earlier today, there was support for the notion that the unemployment insurance program must be tightened up in view of its tremendous cost and its disincentive effect. There was dispute about how this ought to be done, but no proposals made by provincial ministers were offered which, in our view, would have had any different results. No matter what you do, when changes are made to restrict the unemployment insurance program, inevitably you are going to impact on people. I can confirm that the minister gave a clear undertaking that he was willing to consider a softening of the proposal having to do with repeaters in order to take account of the severity of unemployment in particular regions. The minister has not yet worked out the details of this, but he was very sympathetic to the views collectively expressed by the ministers present at the conference.
In so far as any correspondence is concerned, I do not know what the hon. member is referring to. If he can clarify that for me, I will undertake to discuss it with the minister.
